This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a field has a solvable ideal structure, building on a previous finding that these algebras possess nilpotent characteristics. By leveraging a compatible bilinear pair, we establish the solvability of the Zinbien algebra in question, with the level of solvability determined by a specific order dependent on the underlying field characteristics. Notably, when the underlying field possesses a characteristic zero, the solvability order is indefinitely high. Moreover, we establish that a Zinbiel algebra's solvable ideal structure is equivalent to its solvable derivation structure. Lastly, this paper's approach also examines the solvable ideal structure of a related class known as Malcev algebras.

Point process models, such as Poisson autoregressions, have historically been defined as time-independent models with a fixed number of parameters, and have been successfully applied in various contexts including finance, biology, and communication networks. However, these models fail to capture essential characteristics in certain data sets, where the parameters themselves vary over time. To address this limitation, this study introduces a new time-dependent Poisson autoregressive model in which the parameters evolve according to hidden Markov models. We derive an approximate expectation-maximization algorithm for estimating the model's parameters and evaluate the performance of this model on real and artificially generated data sets. Notably, we find that the time-dependent model outperforms its time-independent counterpart when the data exhibits nonstationarity. Moreover, the time-dependent model can be viewed as a hybrid of its time-independent equivalent and hidden Markov models, offering a structured approach that facilitates both parameter reduction and network representation. Moreover, we demonstrate that the time-dependent model can be applied effectively in various scenarios, including credit rating networks, co-expression gene networks, and self-similar traffic networks. The code for the time-dependent Poisson autoregression model is publicly available on GitHub.

Deep learning-based object representations have shown high performance in various tasks, but they struggle when objects are partially occluded, varying in scale, or presented in different orientations. To overcome these limitations, we propose Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that is invariant to orientation and has a continuous output, enabling it to capture variable lengths and scales. We train NDFs to minimize the inter-class variance by matching the distribution of their output elements, achieving state-of-the-art performance in object classification and detection tasks while handling pose, scale, and occlusion. We also introduce a method for predicting 3D bounding boxes from NDFs outputs, which surpasses current baselines in 3D box estimation tasks. Our approach can be trained end-to-end using only 2D annotations, reducing data collection costs. We apply NDFs to various tasks, including point cloud classification, segmentation, and 3D detection from raw images and point clouds, achieving superior results compared to strong baselines. We open-source our code and hope it will benefit the computer vision community.

In 2001, Mezard and Montanari used a complex annealing technique to derive a non-microscopically degenerate solution for random satisfiability problems. They attributed the emergence of a well-defined solution to the presence of a single dominant complex annealing state. Here, we provide an alternative explanation, showing that the presence of a well-defined solution arises from the minimal number of satisfiability variables relative to the random external field. When this ratio is below 1, a dominant complex annealing state does exist, but for ratios of 1 or greater, the complex annealing distribution becomes non-degenerate solely due to the presence of a single dominant real solution. This latter case occurs for all temperatures below a specified threshold, including the critical temperature of the 3-satisfiability problem. To understand this, we first establish the condition under which the complex annealing distribution becomes non-degenerate, and then derive the distribution of the dominant real solution using a statistical physics approach and the Laplace method. This allows us to determine the temperature dependence of the easy-ruin temperature, which marks the onset of a first-order transition in random satisfiability problems. This is in contrast to the previous prediction of a cusp-like behavior at the easy-ruin temperature. Next, we analyze the 3-satisfiability problem and show that the ratio of satisfiability variables to random external field becomes less than 1 only at a higher temperature than predicted by the Bethe ansatz, but still above the alleged algebraic decay temperature of this problem. This indicates that the 3-satisfiability problem experiences a first-order transition with a thermal exponent of 1 and a surface exponent of 3, rather than algebraic decay. This is further confirmed by an estimate of the correlation length, which shows that it increases with temperature as $\sim 0.6/\sqrt{1-T_c}$. This allows us to determine the critical temperature and estimate the easy-ruin temperature and the temperature of the onset of a non-Poisson distribution of unsatisfied clauses as $\sim 1.5\cdot 10^{-3}$. This provides a more detailed understanding of the thermal behavior near the critical temperature of the 3-satisfiability problem. This is achieved without any fit parameters by analyzing the complex annealing distribution as if it were a Poisson process, which allows us to determine the temperature dependence of the easy-ruin temperature and the onset of a non-Poisson distribution of unsatisfied clauses. Recently introduced DoF estimation techniques via image pairs hold promise
for real-world applications but are largely experimental due to limited public
data. To overcome this challenge, this paper introduces a novel, fully automatic
method called DeepHMap++ to estimate pose DoF from single images. DeepHMap++ builds
upon the foundation of a clustering-based projection technique that groups images
by projected views, and a correspondence learning network that identifies matching
regions. To estimate pose DoF from a single image, the proposed framework selects
the most suitable cluster and corresponding projection, thereby determining the
pose DoF. To evaluate DoF estimation, we introduced a novel assessment metric that
measures pose distribution accuracy, in addition to pose estimation and 3D reconstruction
analysis. Experimental results show that DeepHMap++ achieves superior performance in
both pose estimation and 2D-3D correspondence compared to state-of-the-art methods.
To demonstrate the applicability of DeepHMap++ to real-world scenarios, we conducted
a driving simulation experiment and found that it efficiently estimates pose DoF from
single images with limited occlusion. To further challenge the method, we gathered
a large public dataset consisting of 10 different object categories and varied
scenarios but found that current deep learning-based DoF estimation techniques require
more robust object recognition to achieve practical applications. To facilitate
further research, we openly provide the dataset, code, and evaluation tool on websites.

To accurately simulate complex molecular configurations and dynamics, it is essential to efficiently sample configurational space while maintaining precise energy control. This study introduces the Mean Force Langevin Dynamics Sampling (MFLDS) method, which seamlessly combines Langevin dynamics with a harmonic potential to rapidly explore configurational spaces while minimizing computational expenses. By leveraging the stability of harmonic potentials and precise energy control, MFLDS effectively reduces configurational simulation periods by several orders of magnitude compared to alternative methods. By utilizing the NVE version of MFLDS, we successfully simulated multi-domain polypeptide chains, achieving domain separations in a few thousand configurational steps, a significant improvement over previous results using alternative methods. By further optimizing the simulation parameters, we demonstrate the potential to simulate larger systems, paving the way for the application of MFLDS to more intricate biomolecular simulations. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively describe the Planck-scale physics. In this paper, we develop a
quantum approach by constructing the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra within the context
of differential forms. This leads to a modified Dirac equation within the $R$-Minkowski spacetime, where the Dirac matrix $\gamma^{\mu}$ is replaced by $\widetilde{\gamma}^{\mu}$. We then solve this modified Dirac equation using a specific choice of the $R$-Minkowski metric. Additionally, we comment on the relationship between this choice and another established formulation of the Dirac equation and propose a possible interpretation of the results. Lastly, we conclude by highlighting the generality of our approach, which allows for any $R$-Minkowski metric, and suggest a related modification to the Yang-Mills quantum field theory.

The ability to create specified quantum states of light, especially coherent states, via quantum-optical catalysis has been theoretically proven. However, achieving this capability with a single-photon catalyst remains uncertain. Here, we investigate the possibility of generating specified coherent phases of light using a single-photon catalyst. By employing a two-mode bosonic catalyst, we demonstrate that it is possible to create specified coherent phases of light in one mode by injecting a single photon into the other mode. Moreover, we provide a practical solution to approximately implement the necessary unitary transformation using a combination of linear optical elements and photon-number renormalization. Consequently, we show that an initially empty mode can be converted into a state with a well-defined coherent phase, effectively acting as a single-photon catalyzer. Finally, we discuss the effectiveness of our proposed scheme, analyze the system's dynamics, and explore the implications for continuous variable quantum teleportation and quantum-optical catalysis. A recent framework combining machine learning and integer programming to create accurate polymer models has shown high levels of precision. Building upon this foundation, we develop a technique that utilizes linear regression to accurately determine the structure of complex polymers. By integrating this predictive model into the existing framework, we enhance the precision of predicted structures while also accounting for chemical constraints. When applied to realistic scenarios, this technique successfully recreates detailed models of polymers with a high degree of accuracy. Compared to a baseline machine learning approach, our technique achieves significantly better results in both precision and recall. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our method can be highly effective when faced with limited data, outperforming baseline methods by a substantial margin. Code-mixing refers to the practice where bilingual or multilingual individuals switch between two or more languages within a single utterance, often blending words, phrases, or sentences from different languages. This phenomenon is particularly prevalent in areas with limited resources, where multiple languages are commonly used. Code-mixing can manifest in various forms, including intra-utterance language switching, where a single utterance contains elements from more than one language, and inter-utterance language switching, where a conversation alternates between different languages for each individual statement. Code-mixing can be viewed as a sign of language proficiency, though it's also linked to cognitive demands and potential difficulties in communication. Despite its prevalence, code-mixing poses a significant challenge for NLP applications, particularly when aiming to create monolingual outputs from multilingual input. Current approaches often treat code-mixing as an anomaly rather than a crucial aspect of the data, which can result in biased models that may perpetuate inequalities. To address these issues, researchers need to develop more nuanced methods that account for the complex relationships between languages, incorporating techniques such as multilingual training, code-mixing classification, and explicit modeling of code-mixing. By doing so, they can create more effective NLP systems for communities where code-mixing is prevalent, effectively capturing the rich linguistic diversity that these societies embody. Code-mixing can be found across various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis, classification, and generation, with different forms and levels of code-mixing present in multiple tasks and datasets. To facilitate further research, we've assembled a comprehensive catalog of code-mixing datasets and tasks across multiple languages, along with practical guidelines for evaluating code-mixing in NLP systems. By tackling the challenges posed by code-mixing, NLP systems can be made more inclusive, capable of harnessing the vast linguistic resources available in multilingual societies. With code-mixing prevalent in spoken dialogue systems, streaming data, and emergency situations, developing effective methods to handle code-mixing is crucial for creating practical and real-world NLP applications. By accounting for code-mixing, researchers can create more robust and general-purpose models that capture the intricate nuances of multilingual languages, enabling a more authentic and effective NLP system that better represents the rich diversity of multilingual communities. To break down the code-mixing barrier, researchers need to develop a deeper understanding of code-mixing, including identifying the different forms it takes, the reasons behind it, and its impact

We also investigate the connection between descriptions produced by different methods and explore whether selecting diverse descriptions through a human benchmark improves our understanding of their differences. We employ a novel approach that combines explicit ratings with analysis of human-produced reference sentences. We gather a large dataset of reference sentences corresponding to individual images. We use this data to compare the diversity of descriptions produced by various automatic image description generation techniques. We discover that the current state-of-the-art techniques produce descriptions that are indistinguishable from a narrow subset of reference sentences assigned to each image. We identify two main limitations of the current approaches: the descriptions produced are limited to a narrow range of reference sentences and we lack a clear, explicit metric to evaluate their quality. We propose potential avenues for improving description quality by broadening the corresponding reference sentences and suggest simple methods to acquire a limited amount of diverse reference sentences for individual images. We make our dataset of reference sentences available for use in further research. Tantalum oxide Ta2O5 is an intriguing material whose properties make it highly suitable for applications in microelectronics and photonic devices. However, understanding and controllable fabrication of its crystal structure pose significant challenges due to the compound's complex nature and the presence of multiple competing phases. We investigated the ground-state lattice structure of Ta2O5 using a combination of first-principles calculations and Monte Carlo simulations. Our results show that Ta2O5's ground-state configuration corresponds to a Ta-dimer arrangement within the Ta2O5-x (x<0.5)O2+O3+O3 lattice, and found that this structure is stable across various oxygen content levels. Moreover, our research reveals that Ta2O5's dimple-like surface structure is a result of the Ta-dimer formation, and that it correlates with the presence of oxygen vacancies. Notably, our findings also indicate that Ta2O5's 2D and 3D dimer arrangements exhibit significant differences in their dielectric breakdown fields, with the 2D configuration displaying approximately 2 times higher field strength than the 3D structure. Consequently, controlling the Ta-dimer arrangement and related oxygen vacancies could provide a means of tailoring Ta2O5's dielectric properties and further advancing its applicability in microelectronic and photonic devices. Lastly, our research suggests that Ta2O5's low-temperature alpha-phase can be reached through both theoretical Monte Carlo and experimental pathways. Experimental verification of our predictions is highly recommended to facilitate further research into this field.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly debated topic in the field of recommender systems.  Most existing methods focus on combining recommendations across multiple domains through techniques such as weighted summation or product fusion.  However, these approaches often rely on the assumption that each domain contributes equally to the combined recommendation.  In practice, some domains may provide more valuable information than others, leading to suboptimal performance.  To address this limitation, we propose a novel Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation framework, known as MSDCR, which identifies the most critical domains and assigns increased importance to them.  We term this approach of assigning heightened significance to crucial domains as the Intensity of Domain Novelty (IDN) phenomenon.  To capture the IDN phenomenon, MSDCR employs a dual-net structure to determine the novelty intensity of each domain and assign enhanced weights accordingly.  Furthermore, to account for the complexity of user preferences across multiple domains, we introduce a dynamic Aspect Preference Learning (APL) mechanism to adaptively identify the most pertinent aspects and assign them varying levels of significance.  We term this approach of assigning differing levels of significance to varying aspects as the Diversity of Domain Aspect (DDA) phenomenon.  To capture the DDA phenomenon, APL mechanism enables users' preferences to be represented as dynamic graphs, with nodes and edges corresponding to aspects and relationships between them, respectively.  We validate the effectiveness of MSDCR through comprehensive experiments on real-world datasets, achieving superior performance compared to state-of-the-art baselines.  We attribute these results to the intrinsic capabilities of the APL mechanism for capturing complex user preferences and the IDN phenomenon of assigning heightened significance to novel domains, which in turn leads to enhanced recommendation accuracy and diversity.  We also provide implementation details, along with code available online, to facilitate replication and further improvement of the proposed approach.  Finally, we outline potential avenues for future research and extensions to the proposed framework.  We term these extensions as the Extensiveness of Domain Novelty (EDN) and Diversity of Domain Preference (DDP) phenomena.  We believe that addressing these challenges will further propel the advancement of cross-domain recommendation systems.  We term the combination of these phenomena as the Comprehensive Aspect Preference (CAP) phenomenon.  We propose solving these challenges using a combination of multi-task learning and graph-based methods, which we term as the Comprehensive Aspect Preference Learning (CAPL) framework. Hypatia.jl is a Julia package that solves equations involving cones, derived from the work of Nesterov and Shlosman. This note provides a brief introduction to conic equations and explains how Hypatia can be utilized to solve these equations with ease. Specifically, we demonstrate how to define and solve equations involving a diverse range of nonconvex cones by leveraging Hypatia's capabilities. Additionally, we offer a concise guide to implementing a specific example using Hypatia. Building upon this foundation, we outline a more comprehensive strategy for utilizing Hypatia to solve a broader class of nonconvex conic programs. By utilizing Hypatia's automated features, users can bypass the intricacies of explicit implementations and instead focus on formulating their problems using the ConicJuMP language. This approach enables seamless interface integration with other solvers and automated validation of user-defined functions. Ultimately, our goal is to encourage users to explore the many features of Hypatia beyond its capacity to solve conic equations. We also outline potential areas for extending Hypatia's capabilities, including support for dynamic equations, validated numerical methods, and interface development for interactive applications. By leveraging Julia's metaprogramming capabilities, we demonstrate how to achieve this goal and provide a blueprint for further development that can be applied to other similar projects. This approach can be applied to other projects and we believe it holds value for the broader scientific computing community. The accuracy of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is crucial for precise medical diagnosis, and poor image quality can lead to critical consequences. As MRI systems become increasingly automated, quality control is becoming a pressing concern. Presently, MRI quality control relies on manual assessments by skilled professionals, but this approach is time-consuming, prone to fatigue, and can result in inconsistent evaluations. Advanced machine learning techniques offer a promising solution to automate MRI assessment, but training models to accurately evaluate new image samples with different acquisition parameters, operating on diverse MRI scanners, and by different scanning protocols is a significant challenge. In this study, a novel approach is proposed to train a deep learning-based model that can efficiently evaluate the adequacy of new MRI data across various scanners, different acquisition protocols, and with varying levels of data quality. The developed model achieves outstanding performance in assessing MRI data on multiple scanners, different protocols, and with varying levels of data quality, surpassing the capabilities of standard reference-based methods. Notably, the proposed technique demonstrates superior performance when compared to a state-of-the-art, condition-specific approach, highlighting its capability to capture general, scanner-independent features. The developed model also exhibits a high level of accuracy in assessing data quality across different protocols and scanners, achieving a generalization performance that is comparable to, if not better than, models trained on specific protocols. The proposed technique offers a versatile model that can be applied across diverse medical imaging scenarios, providing a valuable framework for the automatic assessment of MRI data quality. To evaluate the context understanding of deep object detectors, we introduced a new metric that compares the contexts where an object is present or absent. This metric, which we call the context difference, measures the variation in context where an object is detected versus where it is not, serving as a indicator of a detector's ability to comprehend its context. We tested this metric on a dataset we created, which consists of 20 object classes and their respective context distributions. Our results showed a positive correlation between the context difference and the accuracy of deep object detectors in identifying their respective contexts. Notably, the context where an object is present is, on average, 3.6 times larger than the context where it is absent, based on our dataset. By examining the individual classes, we found that some objects are easily recognized in narrow contexts, whereas others are more readily detected in broader ones. To further explore this, we analyzed the average height of the bounding boxes in our dataset and found a positive linear relationship between this dimension and the width of the context. To improve the performance of object detectors in specific scenarios, our research suggests considering the height of the bounding boxes as an auxiliary training task to expand the context where the object is likely to be present. By doing so, we successfully improved the accuracy of the detector in one of the tested classes by a margin of 4.3%. Our research provides a starting point for evaluating and improving the context understanding of deep object detectors. We have made our code and dataset publicly available on GitHub. When allocating kidneys, a key challenge arises when some offered kidneys don't match any waiting recipient due to blood type incompatibility. This study examines the optimal acceptance policies for kidney donors by analyzing the trade-off between accepting a mismatched kidney now versus waiting for a matched one. By exploring different scenarios with varying levels of waiting time and survival benefits, we identify specific conditions under a specific probability model where accepting a mismatched kidney is optimal. Furthermore, we establish that, in comparison to the commonly used "simultaneous acceptance" rule, a more nuanced policy that takes into account the level of blood type compatibility can lead to better health outcomes for patients while efficiently utilizing available kidneys. By leveraging real data from the United Network for Organ Sharing, we test and validate our findings in a practical setting. Ultimately, our research provides an optimal solution for addressing blood type limitations in kidney allocation and offers a framework for analyzing similar problems in other organ transplantation contexts. By exploring the economic costs of waiting, we also derive a general rule that can be applied to any allocation problem involving waiting and time-dependent risks. Lastly, our study reveals that prioritizing patients with higher levels of blood type compatibility does not necessarily lead to fair outcomes for all patients. By conducting a series of numerical experiments using a Monte Carlo method, we demonstrate that transplanting a mismatched kidney at the optimal time can result in up to a 25% improvement in patient survival rates. By leveraging the concepts of renewal theory, we develop an intuitive yet optimal policy that maximizes long-term patient survival rates by balancing the benefits of transplanted kidneys with the costs of waiting. By testing this policy on real data from the United Network for Organ Sharing, we find that it can lead to a 10% to 15% improvement in patient survival rates. Ultimately, our research provides actionable guidance for healthcare professionals managing kidney transplant waiting lists and can be applied to similar organ allocation problems. By utilizing a level-set method to define the interface between phases and an embedded boundary technique to handle boundary interactions, we've developed a numerical approach that efficiently handles moving boundaries and accurately represents the interface without mesh constraints. A direct application method has been devised to directly compute the normal velocity of the interface without resolving the velocity field, reducing the need for additional storage and computational resources. A simplified representation of the interface has been utilized to determine the boundary conditions on solid surfaces, enabling efficient numerical solution in problems involving contact lines and melting/solidification. A validated numerical scheme has been developed and applied to test problems, including melting and solidification scenarios, droplet interaction, and Stefan problems. A higher-order level-set method has been integrated into the approach to enhance the accuracy of the results. A comparative analysis with existing level-set methods has been performed to evaluate the numerical performance of the introduced approach. In complex multiplayer games with multiple agents, understanding how each player's decision-making process interacts with others to reach a equilibrium state is crucial, but often such interactions result in opaque relationships that impede learning and policy design. Typically, games with large player interactions are modeled using strategic equilibrium frameworks like Nash Equilibrium, yet computing and learning from these equilibria is computationally expensive and challenging, especially when the number of players is large. In our research, we introduce a novel framework called Explainable Markov Games by Potential Reverse Engineering (EMG-PRE) that leverages a unique combination of potential regression and reverse engineering to provide a linear logarithmic size explanation for each player's behavior, enabling us to design policies that learn from and benefit from these explanations. We demonstrate how this understanding can be utilized to develop a variety of high-quality policies, including those that address concerns about sustainability and fairness. When compared to baseline policies, our proposed solutions result in a notable improvement in performance, with gains of up to 97% observed in certain tests. Our novel framework EMG-PRE also offers a range of practical policy design applications that do not rely on the original game's explicit representation, utilizing the introduced explanation as a key component that helps guide learning, as shown through multiple fairness-themed scenarios. We evaluate and validate our framework on a range of games with both small and large player interactions, utilizing both simple and complex models to predict each player's individual behavior. Overall, our research provides a groundbreaking approach to enhancing the ability to learn and design policies in complex multiplayer games, with the added benefit of significantly reducing the required computational resources. With modifications, this approach can also be applied to similar learning-based games that involve strategic decision-making. We offer the code for our proposed method at the URL https://github.com/chenziangjie/EMG-PRE.

To improve the effectiveness of experience replay, Variance Reduction Replay (VDR) is proposed as a technique to enhance policy optimization. By applying the variance diminution method, VDR calculates a weighted average of the loss derived from a batch of data, which reduces the variance and accelerates policy optimization. Unlike existing methods that utilize a fixed importance weight, VDR dynamically adjusts the weights based on the gradient distribution, thereby preventing over-sharpening of the policy and minimizing the occurrence of policy stagnation. By enhancing the policy optimization process through variance reduction, VDR is shown to improve the performance of several challenging benchmark tasks, surpassing the results obtained with the vanilla policy optimization method. Moreover, VDR is computationally efficient and can be seamlessly integrated with existing policy optimization frameworks, resulting in significant improvements in various benchmark settings. The code for VDR has been made publicly available on GitHub. By leveraging the variance reduction technique, VDR achieves a data-efficient approach to approximately linear exploration, which is essential for scaling policy optimization to complex, high-dimensional domains. The official title of this paper is Variance Diminution based Experience Replay for Policy Optimization but it is published under the VDR name.

Presently available dialogue evaluation frameworks fall short in assessing a single speaker's ability to participate in multiple branches of a conversation. To address this limitation, we present a highly branching dialogue evaluation framework, where speakers can interact with various branches of a conversation. Each branch represents a self-contained discussion with a unique goal, and our framework evaluates speakers' ability to navigate these branches by selecting appropriate responses. To encourage diverse conversations, our framework incorporates a diversity penalty, which discourages speakers from repeating the same response in similar conversation branches. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our diversity penalty in promoting varied conversations and showcase multiple evaluation metrics that capture a speaker's performance in different branches of a conversation. These metrics include a diversity score, a relevance score, a coherence score, and a satisfaction ratio, all of which can be adjusted by the user to suit their evaluation needs. To facilitate widespread adoption, we provide pre-trained models of approximately 5 million parameters, which can be fine-tuned for a wide range of tasks by dialogue system developers. Our evaluation framework is available online, along with sample dialogue scripts, evaluation metrics, and trained models. We envision applications of our framework in evaluating spoken dialogue systems that involve multiple speakers, such as group meetings and multi-agent dialogue systems. This approach allows us to efficiently explore a wide range of parameters in these theories through smaller simulations, which can then be rapidly scaled up to match the comprehensive results of full simulations. We apply and test this method for two types of modified gravity theories: f(R) models with a specific parameter modification, which we find produce identical cosmological simulations when matched in certain conditions. We also explore a range of simulation scenarios to assess the method's applicability and accuracy. Leveraging this technique, we create a set of large N-body simulation results for the $f(R)$ models with a specific parameter modification, which can be utilized as proxies for comparable simulations in other modified gravity theories, such as $e/A$ and $μ$-dark matter. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections exist and describe the driving forces as asymptotic log-gas systems on compact contours within these domains. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the statistics of the SLE curves and the underlying Riemann surface, as well as the behavior of the imaginary surfaces and the SLE system as the system grows without bound. Furthermore, we establish that, in the half-plane case, the statistics of the SLE curve determine the underlying Riemann surface, which is equivalent to a known result proven by Dubédat using different methods. We derive the explicit formulas for the mean velocity and pairing operator of the system in the half-plane case. We also explore the behavior of the system as the beta parameter approaches 2, finding that it becomes related to the Trubetzkoy-Bieberbach metric and ultimately approaches a constant as beta equals 2. We show that, in the half-plane case, the system can be obtained as a scaling limit from a random lattice of interacting Loewner driving functions, and we determine the characteristics of this scaling limit. We end by discussing some open questions about the subject. We believe that the log-gas perspective may provide a more general framework for studying the statistics of SLE curves and the associated imaginary surfaces. We also propose a conjecture about the behavior of the system in the quarter-plane case. We discuss three possible scenarios for this behavior and offer some supporting evidence for each of the three possible outcomes. We further explore the relationship between the system in the half-plane case and the Bessel line ensemble, as well as the statistics of the pairings and the local statistics of the system in the quarter-plane case. We also examine the relationship between the system in the half-plane case and the Airy line ensemble. Nonlocal gravity represents a general theoretical framework that effectively describes the effects of higher powers of gravity and encompasses a range of scalar gravitational theories as a particular aspect. This paper focuses on a specific nonlocal gravity model characterized by a particular nonlocal operator that can be variational in nature. By applying the DeWitt-Schwartz formalism, we investigate the nonlocal operator's properties and derive the constitutive relations for the nonlocal gravity field. The constitutive relations are found to resemble those obtained using the Lorentz non-invariant version of the Einstein power, however with an added non-local contribution that arises from varying the nonlocal operator rather than the Einstein action. The implications of these results on gravity saturation and nonlocal effects during binary mergers are also examined. The approach employed in this paper can be applied to nonlocal gravity models involving vector and tensor nonlocal gravity. The constitutive relations derived from these models are then used to determine the nonlocal effects on the degeneracy of binary neutron star mergers. Understanding how and where genetic elements influence specific traits or functions within an organism has led to the integration of genome-wide association study data and genomic features such as gene expression, DNA element usage, and chromatin structure. These analyses have been conducted for individual traits but have not been collectively examined to identify patterns of association with genetic elements. Here, a comprehensive analysis was performed that simultaneously explored the relationship between genetic elements and eighteen different traits or functions using data from the ENCODE project, in conjunction with large-scale genetic association studies. This study utilized a comprehensive database of genetic elements and association regions associated with eighteen different traits or functions, and further incorporated data on the usage of DNA elements, gene expression levels, and histone modification patterns across multiple cell types and tissues. The results revealed a distinct correlation between the usage of DNA elements and the majority of the associated regions (approximately 70%) across all eighteen different traits or functions. Furthermore, variations in gene expression levels were observed among the associated regions, with approximately one-third (approximately 30%) exhibiting a significant association with the traits or functions. In contrast, approximately ten percent (approximately 10%) of the associated regions showed minimal expression levels. This study demonstrated that the majority of associated regions across all eighteen different traits or functions are influenced by the same set of genetic elements, with the exception of specific tissue or cell-type dependent elements such as those found in muscle tissue or lymphoid cells. In conclusion, this study has provided a comprehensive framework for understanding the relationship between genetic elements and the associated regions across all eighteen different traits or functions, with implications for further research into the mechanisms governing the influence of genetic elements on specific traits or functions. In addition, this study has identified areas for improving the power and accuracy of genome-wide association studies, with potential applications in the efficient selection of associated regions and the integration of data from multiple cell types and tissues. This study has also been made available as a public resource for further research into the complex mechanisms governing the influence of genetic elements on specific traits or functions. This study has been physically hosted at the ENCODE project website. Combining these, the QCD color field framework, known as the "minor system" approach, allows researchers to describe the quark gluon plasma produced in heavy-ion and proton-lead collisions and compare them to small and large systems in proton-proton collisions. This comparison can reveal the influence of initial state effects and help identify the minimum size or "huler horizon" where a system can be considered a state of its own, as opposed to being a part of a larger system. This contribution reviews the concept of the "minor system" and its potential to advance our understanding of the interface between small and large systems in the strong interaction. Additionally, it presents preliminary findings from the LHC regarding the characteristics of the most likely "minor systems" that give rise to the small and large systems studied in proton-proton collisions. These include systems with a specific charge or mass that exhibit characteristics similar to those of the small and large systems in proton-proton collisions. If confirmed, these results have the potential to significantly advance our understanding of the strong interaction.

Overlooking the role of momentum-dependent electron-phonon and spin-phonon interactions may lead to an inaccurate prediction of heat tolerance in materials. By examining these interactions in depth, we have derived a general expression that accounts for their dynamic effects and incorporated it into a strategy for determining whether a material can withstand high temperatures. Utilizing this approach, we have investigated the thermal stability of graphene, a material known for its exceptional strength and conductivity, and discovered both static and dynamic fluctuations that threaten its structural integrity and conductivity. Our analysis highlights the significance of considering momentum-dependent interactions and the vital role they play in predicting the thermal stability and conductivity of graphene and similar materials. Our findings suggest that a minor adjustment to graphene's lattice structure can greatly enhance its thermal stability and conductivity, and that this approach can be applied to other materials with more complex structures. When engaging in conversations, individuals frequently encounter diverse semantics.
From straightforward facts like "Paris is the capital of France," to more abstract connections
like "If someone believes that all students did poorly, they likely think that not all
students excelled." Such pragmatic understanding of dialogue is rarely addressed in NLP.
Our proposed Semantic Variety Dialogue Dataset (SVDD) bridges this gap by integrating
pragmatic elements with Inference-based dialogue.
In SVDD, one participant establishes an inference connection with another, whose level
of semantic understanding remains unknown.
The speaking participant aims to guide the listening participant to a specific inference
relation through relevant information.
Our evaluation reveals that current state-of-the-art language models struggle with SVDD,
primarily due to the unknown level of semantic variety.
To address this challenge, we introduce a variety-aware objective that assesses the
unknown level of semantic variety as unknown, and find it to be a critical factor in
improving the effectiveness of SVDD.
When applied to SVDD, it enhances the performance by approximately 10%.
Our proposed approach and additional evaluation tasks demonstrate the versatility
of variety-aware objectives in tackling diverse Inference-based tasks.

The up-to-date understanding of hot Jupiters suggests that their large size and moderate temperature are a result of migrating planets that experienced high surface temperatures during their formation. This theory is supported by calculations showing that the interior temperatures of 30 MJ (mass of Jupiter) or more massive planets are too high for stable solidification, leaving behind only small, fully molten cores. This study simulates the development and dying breath of low-mass, rotating stars with 0.1 to 10 times the mass of Jupiter using one-dimensional hydrodynamic and nuclear reaction models. It finds that the duration of convection in these objects is very short, with temperatures and luminosities reaching peak levels within a day. As they run out of fuel, all objects with masses above 10.5 MJ (based on their initial mass) eventually shed their outer layers before dying, with the remaining cores being similar in size to the cores of more massive hot Jupiters. This research suggests that the solidification of fully molten cores may take longer than previously thought, with estimates ranging from thousands to millions of years, and cores may remain molten even below 10 MJ, with fully molten cores being found in objects with masses as low as 5.5 MJ. This study also explores the interplay between mass loss and the duration of a star's life, finding that the mass lost by the dying star is directly related to its initial mass, with objects with masses above 7.5 MJ losing more than half their mass before dying. A valued domain (R, M) is defined to have a total residue map if every element in R has a maximal ideal whose residue corresponds to all of R's maximal ideals. We establish that this property is conserved when extending from a polynomial ring to a rational function field. Additionally, we demonstrate that a domain (R, M) that is algebraically closed has a total residue map when it contains a domain of Krull dimension one that, in turn, has a total residue map. As a result, we are able to prove the known fact that such a domain is integrally closed. We also provide an alternative proof for the fact that a domain with a total residue map is integrally closed when it contains a domain of Krull dimension one that, in turn, has a total residue map, by using the fact that being integrally closed is equivalent to being algebraically unconnected under the rational function field scenario. We conclude by examining the integral closure of a domain with a total residue map when it contains a domain of Krull dimension one. As an example, we examine the integral closure of the polynomial ring $k[x,y]/(xy-1)$ and find that it is equivalent to the integral closure of the rational function field $k(x,y)/\langle x,y\rangle$ within its total quotient ring. We discover that this latter ring is equivalent to the rational function field $\bigl(\bigl(k(x)\bigr)^{\text{alg}}\bigr)^3\bigr)/\langle x_1x_2,x_1x_3,x_2x_3\rangle$ and find that it has dimension $6$ and is not integrally closed, thus providing an alternative to the example given in \cite{Hun}. We also examine the integral closure of the polynomial ring $k[x,y]/(f(x,y))$ where $f(x,y)$ is a non-constant polynomial of any degree and it is irreducible over the algebraic closure of $k$. We find that the integral closure of this latter ring is equivalent to the rational function field $k(x,y)/\langle x,y\rangle$ within its total quotient ring. We conclude by examining the relationship between being algebraically closed and having a total residue map when considering the extension from a rational function field to a rational function field in multiple variables. The growing need to lower electricity consumption in data centers propels the exploration of a new technique called frequency degradation. By deliberately narrowing the CPU frequency, we aim to achieve both performance improvement and significant energy reduction. Building upon prior research in frequency degradation, this paper takes a more substantial step, advocating for a much broader range of reduced frequencies (10 to 50 times lower) and a new method called "degraded execution time" to gauge the suitable frequency reduction. We also develop a critical threshold for which performance starts to decline and explore various workloads through two different scenarios, including both small and large-scale reductions in frequency. Ultimately, this paper demonstrates the applicability of a very substantial frequency reduction (around 25 times lower) in real-world settings, resulting in both notable performance gains (up to 25%) and considerable energy savings (up to 60%). To facilitate widespread adoption, we openly provide the HyperDegrade tool used in this research.

In the field of robot motion planning, specifically for manipulating links of various types, a crucial task is to determine whether two given links can be distinguished, or are identical and share the same configuration. This distinction is crucial for further analysis in motion planning, as it affects the calculation of relative motions and configuration spaces. In general, determining the difference between two links involves solving a system of polynomial equations, which can be time-consuming and difficult to solve, especially when dealing with links of a complex nature, such as those with multiple joints. In contrast, we propose a new and more efficient method, known as the "disentangling operation," which can determine the difference between two links by utilizing a simpler mathematical approach based on polynomial functions and ring theory, thus providing a more streamlined analysis for motion planning algorithms. In addition, this method can be easily integrated into existing frameworks for analyzing and comparing links, offering a versatile and adaptable tool for a broad range of applications in robotics and beyond. In particular, we demonstrate how this method can be applied to examine the uniqueness of configurations in granular materials, which are characterized by multiple contact points between grains and require complex calculations to determine contact relationships and differentiate grains. By leveraging the disentangling operation, we can simplify these calculations and provide a more direct path to identifying unique configurations and determining contact relationships between grains. In the context of granular materials and other complex systems with multiple contacts, this method offers a valuable insight into the fundamental problem of distinguishing individual elements within a system that is characterized by diverse and dynamic relationships between its components. In the broader context of mathematics and its applications to science and engineering, this method provides a new perspective on the use of ring theory in analyzing and solving problems in physics and robotics, offering a new avenue for further research and development. In the specific case of granular materials, this method can be used to examine the uniqueness of configurations and determine contact relationships between grains, which is crucial for accurately predicting the behavior and stability of granular materials under various loads and stresses. In tasks that involve concurrent synchronization across multiple tasks, each executed by a different robot, we examine optimal strategies for sequencing and timing to maximize overall performance. By leveraging a new method that values the benefits of delayed completion, we establish that there is only one optimal policy for robot tasks, including those that require synchronization, sequencing, and time-based decisions. By applying this approach in a controlled setting, we gather data on the ideal synchronization times. Utilizing these results, we create a control policy that maximizes performance and remains within predetermined boundaries. When applied to random configurations of robots, this policy produces outcomes that closely match expected performance, as validated by statistical testing. Finally, we explore various network variations to demonstrate how our policy adapts to different network scenarios. Overall, our study provides a framework and key findings that can be used to optimize performance in complex tasks across networks of robots.

While federated learning is gaining popularity, ensuring data privacy remains a pressing concern.  To address this issue, several secure federated learning protocols have been proposed, such as federated learning with untruthful users and multi-party FL, which can resist dishonest participants who manipulate the training process for their own benefit.  However, in this paper, we show that both FL with untruthful users and multi-party FL can be compromised through non-malicious means.  Specifically, we have discovered two privacy-invasive attacks that compromise the security of these protocols without any malicious intent.  By deliberately revealing additional information about the data used for training, we have found that it is possible to diminish the model's accuracy with negligible data-sharing costs.  Our experiment, which involved training a model on vertically partitioned data, showed that sharing just one more kilobyte of data could result in a 10% decline in accuracy.  To counter these privacy assaults, we have developed a new privacy-preserving protocol that is more resilient against such attacks and still maintains the efficiency of secure federated learning.  Our proposed solution has been put to the test and has shown superior performance in comparison to the baseline protocols.  When implemented on a dataset that consists of one million samples, our protocol was capable of achieving classification accuracy of over 95% within just five rounds of training.  Moreover, our solution has the added benefit of being applicable to a broad spectrum of machine learning applications.  In conclusion, the discovery of these privacy assaults on secure federated learning highlights the significance of considering new privacy concerns that could arise during the training process.  By acknowledging these concerns, we have developed a secure federated learning protocol that is more resilient against such privacy-invasive attacks and has the added benefit of being highly efficient, making it suitable for complex machine learning models that consist of millions of parameters.  In addition to its suitability for complex machine learning models, our proposed solution has the added benefit of being highly adaptable to a broad spectrum of machine learning applications, from linear models to deep neural networks.  In our experiment, we successfully trained a deep neural network on a dataset that consisted of one million samples within just ten rounds of training.  The developed protocol has been found to be highly resilient against the privacy assaults and has been shown to minimize the shared data while maintaining the accuracy of the model, resulting in a data-sharing cost that is nearly optimal. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. To overcome this limitation, the use of Random Fourier Features has gained popularity by transforming high-dimensional kernel functions into low-dimensional dot products, thereby significantly reducing computational costs. However, this method has a crucial drawback: it results in the loss of important data-dependent characteristics in feature transformations, which are critical for achieving superior performance. To address this shortcoming, we propose a novel method that reinstates data-dependent characteristics by creating multiple feature maps and aggregating them based on the input data. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed approach on several classification and regression tasks using popular kernel-based learning algorithms, and our method outperforms the standard Random Fourier Features method in terms of both accuracy and training time. We also explore the relationship between our proposed approach and standard Random Fourier Features and discuss its limitations. Experimentally, we show that our proposed method is particularly beneficial when data lies in a nonlinear manifold. To train our proposed method, we provide an efficient batch-based update strategy to address memory constraints when working with large datasets. We also discuss and evaluate three different batch-based update strategies. We further investigate and discuss the connection between our proposed method and other kernel approximation techniques, finding that our approach is distinct from existing methods. To facilitate real-world applications, we have made our proposed method compatible with popular machine learning frameworks, and we provide comprehensive experimental evaluations on multiple datasets using these frameworks, along with reproducibility code. Along with the proposed method, we have also explored and evaluated two alternative batch-based update strategies and found that our default approach consistently yields superior results. We believe that our proposed method offers a versatile and adaptable kernel approximation technique that is applicable to a broad spectrum of machine learning tasks and algorithms. Along with the proposed method, we have also explored and evaluated the role of regularization in kernel approximation and found that it is a critical factor in achieving optimal results. We have also explored and evaluated the proposed method on multiple linear and nonlinear regression tasks and found that it is capable of accurately capturing complex underlying relationships between variables. Along with the proposed method, we have also evaluated and compared the results with multiple baseline kernel approximation techniques and found that our proposed method yields superior results in terms of both accuracy and training time. Along with the proposed method, we have also evaluated and compared the results with standard Random Fourier Features and found that our proposed method yields data-dependent kernel estimates, which is a critical advantage over the standard Random Fourier Features approach.

In our study, we establish a precise criterion for a permutation group to be embedded within a direct product of isomorphic wreath products through a compatible system of monomial embeddings. This condition is equivalent to each component of the direct product satisfying a individual, independently defined condition. We further demonstrate that this condition is met if the original group exhibits a specific property called resolvable transitivity. Additionally, our research provides an alternative proof of a previously established result by Cameron and Li. Lastly, our work offers an improvement upon an earlier theorem by Li by removing the requirement for a specific subgroupal structure.

We investigate conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n ≥ 2) within the (n+2)-dimensional sphere, exploring how these surfaces can be locally defined through the Moebius operator in relation to their scalar curvatures. By applying the operator, we discover that the Moebius curvature can be distinguished from the original curvature by a specific factor, which, in turn, enables us to establish equivalence classes based on this relationship. We further establish that these classes are consistent with another established classification method. Additionally, we establish the uniqueness of specific hypersurface types that achieve maximum, minimum, or specific average Moebius curvatures, building upon previous research by the first author. We also explore and analyze the average Moebius curvature of these hypersurfaces, discovering its connection to the mean curvature and surface area, which in turn allows us to establish necessary and sufficient criteria for these hypersurfaces to have maximum, minimum, or specific average Moebius curvatures. We conclude by examining the implications of these findings for related research areas.

Researchers studying the dynamics of complex systems have employed network damage models as a tool for analysis. A special class of models called "avalanche" or "sandpile" models simulate the gradual failure of systems under external stress by transferring material from one location to another in response to excess height. The resulting distribution of the sizes of these failures, known as the "magnitude distribution," holds significant insight into the stability and robustness of the system. To better understand the statistical properties of these systems, researchers have typically turned to random network structures. However, our research involves examining the dynamics of avalanche systems on a unique type of network called Cayley trees, which have a hierarchical structure, for the first time. By simulating these systems using the Bak-Sneppen model and others, we have derived precise mathematical formulas to describe the distribution of failure sizes, which can be validated through computational simulations. These findings can be applied to real-world scenarios, such as geophysical systems, by testing how changes to the rules governing the system's evolution affect its behavior and properties. One interesting discovery revealed that the distribution of failure sizes follows a power law with a specific exponent of 3.5, which can also be influenced by the presence of external stress. By exploring different models and adapting them to fit the structure of Cayley trees, we have gained a deeper understanding of how the distribution of failure sizes is affected by various parameters, which can be compared to the results obtained using random network structures. One notable exception, the Hasting model, failed to produce a power-law distribution of failure sizes. One potential application of these findings involves interpreting the results in the context of real-world systems, which can be represented as complex networks with spatial relationships between elements. One way to achieve this involves reinterpreting the models in terms of their original physical meanings, which can be challenging but also rewarding as it may uncover new insights into the underlying dynamics of these systems. One such example involves the Bak-Sneppen model, which can be seen as a representation of the geological process of erosion, which constantly rearranges the landscape by removing the lowest point and creating a new point at the same height. The detection of gravitational waves by advanced detectors is significantly limited in the high-frequency range by the quantum noise effect caused by laser light interacting with free masses. Overcoming this constraint is crucial for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We propose a novel interferometer design called the sloshing-Sagnac topology, which incorporates a new mass oscillation source to counteract the impact of laser light on masses and thus reduces the influence of quantum noise. By utilizing this design, we find that a advanced LIGO-like sloshing-Sagnac interferometer would have a 4 times greater sensitivity at high frequencies than the standard advanced LIGO detector. This improved sensitivity would allow the detector to identify gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers with total masses up to 25 solar masses. We also examine the design's applicability to future detectors such as Einstein Telescope, finding that a 3 km Einstein Telescope with a sloshing-Sagnac topology would have a frequency range that extends down to 5 Hz, surpassing the goal of detecting gravitational waves in the entire band used by pulsar timing arrays. This research demonstrates the potential of the sloshing-Sagnac topology in improving the sensitivity of future gravitational wave detectors to the high-frequency range. This design's effectiveness in combating backaction noise also makes it a promising solution for other applications that rely on the conversion of optical signals to mechanical motion. Recently, Extreme Large-MIMO systems have garnered significant interest, and their potential to prevent inter-user interference through unique visibility regions in the raster scan protocol have been found to be highly beneficial. Research has shown that up to half of the available time slots can be saved in XL-MIMO systems by only allowing access to users with non-overlapping visibility regions. However, the protocol's effectiveness is contingent upon the specific arrangement of users and their corresponding visibility regions. This paper delves into the statistical analysis of random XL-MIMO system configurations, aiming to determine the average overlap percentage of visibility regions for certain grid-based arrangements. It has been discovered that square arrangements yield the highest average overlap, with approximately 49% of the time slots being saved, whereas rectangular and triangular configurations exhibit significantly lower average overlap percentages. Additionally, a method has been established to track the development of visibility regions over time, enabling further exploration into various temporal system configurations.

Researchers studied the properties of dense matter using relativistic mean-field theory with a vector meson's coupling modified to mimic "soft" or "stiff" behavior similar to that observed in neutron stars. By adjusting the vector meson's coupling, a range of "soft" values was found to result in neutron stars with masses similar to that of the Sun, whereas "stiff" values led to more massive stars with up to 2.8 times the sun's mass. However, only the "stiff" case can explain the high density of matter observed in rotating neutron stars. When applied to finite nuclei, the "stiff" approach yielded a better fit to measured densities of certain nuclei, particularly those with high neutron excess like $^{40}$Ca, $^{48}$Ca, $^{72}$Kr, $^{100}$Mo, $^{132}$Sn, and $^{208}$Pb. Additionally, this "stiff" behavior was found to be consistent with the observed characteristics of rotating neutron stars and supernovae remnants, with a magnetic field strength similar to that of the "Big Apple" (approximately 10 to the power of 13) and a spin frequency similar to that of PSR B1534+12 (approximately 1.4 kilohertz). If confirmed, this "stiff" density distribution could have significant implications for nuclear physics and astrophysics, offering a possible explanation for the measured densities of finite nuclei, the composition of rotating neutron stars, and the high energy output observed in some supernovae remnants. This could also provide a foundation for a new approach to describing the properties of finite and infinite nuclear matter using a single, self-consistent theory. This study's results agree with previous findings showing that the measured densities of finite nuclei are consistent with a specific density distribution, and it extends this understanding to infinite nuclear matter and rotating neutron stars. To address this issue, a strategy is proposed to create frequency-stable gates by balancing the driving frequencies of multiple modes, thus eliminating the need for precise synchronization. This approach, which is applicable to both small and large-scale systems, has been experimentally validated using a setup with two trapped ions and demonstrates the successful implementation of a $\pi$-gate up to 20 dB below the optimal signal strength without significant precision loss. Researchers have explored the NA62 experiment at CERN to enhance sensitivity in detecting a specific process involving the creation of heavy neutral leptons during the decay of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$. By analyzing various heavy neutral lepton masses, we found that the NA62 detector's efficiency for detecting these particles peaks at an electron momentum of 50 GeV, and that the introduction of additional cuts related to photon detection lowers the detection sensitivity for heavy neutral leptons with masses greater than 10 MeV. Neural language models have significantly outperformed $n$-gram models in various applications but suffer from limited domain adaptability. In contrast, $n$-gram models excel in this regard due to their data shift sensitivity but are computationally expensive and prone to overfitting. We leverage the strengths of both models to create a hybrid approach, incorporating a neural network to generate a subset of training data and combining it with a learned dataset from $n$-gram models using transfer learning. We call this method NGRAM, and through extensive experiments, it demonstrates enhanced performance, a broader domain adaptation range, and a 2 times speedup in inference compared to conventional neural language models. NGRAM's versatility enables it to be applicable in various tasks such as data pretraining, generation, and token filling. Moreover, we introduce a new evaluation metric called Effective Data Size (EDS), accurately capturing the data efficiency of different models. NGRAM exhibits superior EDS scores compared to baseline neural models, confirming its efficiency in reducing training and inference data. NGRAM's source code is publicly available at this link: https://github.com/ChangKun/NGRAM.

The storage's ability to accomplish this task is hindered by its risk-averse nature, which causes it to avoid absorbing variance in electricity prices. To counter this, an optimal self-allocation method for the storage system across various locations within a market is necessary. In this research, we develop a storage allocation framework that takes into account the risks and uncertainties of changing electricity prices, with the goal of minimizing overall system costs. By leveraging convex optimization and stochastic linear programming techniques, we design an incentive-compatible, decentralized mechanism that enables individual storage systems to prioritize their own risk preferences while participating in a community-level storage allocation strategy. This results in a storage allocation that optimally manages both production and consumption within a system, even in the presence of external shocks. To validate this approach, we conduct numerical experiments using real-world data from Germany's electricity market. These experiments demonstrate that, with an appropriate storage allocation mechanism, a risk-averse storage system can effectively manage its own risk and maximize its own benefits, ultimately leading to improved overall system performance. This achievement is made possible by the storage's ability to manage local supply and demand within a neighborhood, which in turn allows it to manage both internal and external risks more effectively. Researchers who utilize silicon-based donors for quantum computing are concerned about the potential for nearby silicon defects to influence performance. Specifically, the effect of the silicon divacancy needs to be understood as it is highly prevalent and difficult to eradicate. This study utilizes accurate simulations to examine how a single silicon divacancy interacts with individual donors by modeling various positions, orientations, and charge states. Combining these simulations with a quantum gate operator, we demonstrate how to incorporate the influence of a nearby silicon divacancy into the calculation of a two-qubit state. This approach has been put into practice, yielding valuable insights into the behavior of a single silicon divacancy and enabling effective description of its impact on a nearby donor. We have made the simulation data available and plan to expand the simulation to a 50-valley effective mass theory. By doing so, we hope to make the simulation more accurate and applicable to real-world scenarios. This study has significant implications for the placement of quantum gates in silicon-based donors and highlights the difficulty of removing the silicon divacancy, a challenge that may need to be actively managed through targeted implantation or thermal treatment. This could be achieved by positioning the divacancy outside of the quantum volume, where its influence on the donor is reduced when it occupies a doubly charged state but where it still occupies a singly charged state that may interact with the donor through its larger orbital and where it may also bind to other nearby donors, forming a quantum-linked donor-divacancy center. This study suggests that further research is necessary to develop efficient methods for removing the silicon divacancy, including the use of targeted thermal treatment, silicon isotopes, or implantation of divacancy precursors. Our investigation focused on conducting an exhaustive analysis of quantum conduction within HgTe quantum wells that have a nearly gapless energy spectrum, using a comprehensive quantum mechanical approach. By applying a variational method to optimize the well width, we determined the optimal dimensions for these wells, finding that they should have a width of approximately 6.5 nm to minimize scattering off phonons and interface disorder. Next, we examined the influence of phonon and impurity scattering on the quantum states, taking into account the unique properties of the nearly gapless energy spectrum. We discovered that phonon scattering exerts a more substantial impact on scattering probability compared to impurity scattering due to the small energy gap. Additionally, we identified that phonon and impurity scattering primarily affect the Kramers-degenerate pairs in the nearly gapless energy spectrum, leading to a breakdown of this degeneracy and resulting in a small energy gap. We were also able to calculate this energy gap as a function of well width and found that it alternates between an indirect and a direct transition as the width changes, mediated by combined effects of combined elastic and potential disorder. We further explored the influence of non-abrupt well interfaces on the energy spectrum and the resulting scattering, finding that they can mimic the effect of combined elastic and potential disorder, including alternating between an indirect and a direct transition as the interface smoothness changes. We also examined the scattering within semi-elastic Raman scattering processes and found that it can be significantly reduced by selecting the laser energy accordingly. We calculated the optimal range for this purpose and found that it depends on the well width. We also calculated the resulting carrier distribution, scattering probability, and the resulting energy gaps as a function of laser energy, providing a quantitative analysis of the conditions necessary to minimize scattering and reduce carrier distribution in these systems. To facilitate the analysis, we introduce a new metric called the "learning gap", which assesses the existence of an equilibrium where players can gain by learning derivatives. To achieve a deeper understanding of the properties of quarks and gluons, which comprise approximately 80% of the matter within our universe, it is necessary to study high-energy collisions involving protons and nuclei. While such studies have been successfully conducted using proton-proton and heavy-ion collisions, there is currently a lack of data available for proton-nucleus interactions. This study aims to develop a detection method for identifying top quark production in such collisions, which is challenged by the high background levels typical of these events. By utilizing advanced reconstruction techniques and optimized selection criteria for sub-jets and lepton combinations, it is demonstrated that top quarks can be detected with a p-value of less than 10^-5, thus paving the way for experimental verification of top quark production in proton-nucleus collisions. Furthermore, this study in heavy-flavor physics provides a unique opportunity to calibrate the properties of heavy quarks in small systems, which is crucial for accurately interpreting data from heavy-ion collisions. A generic cut-and-merge method is also introduced to facilitate efficient computations of sub-jet multiplicities in heavy-flavor production. By leveraging existing knowledge of heavy-flavor distribution functions, it is possible to predict the production rates of charm and bottom quarks in proton-nucleus collisions, thus enabling the development of precise detection strategies for these particles. These predictions can be compared to data from heavy-ion collisions and used to validate the properties of quarks and gluons. These findings have significant implications for ongoing and future experiments, such as the ALICE, CMS, ATLAS, LHCb, and future experiments like the sPHESIGS and the ALICEnext detectors, which are capable of accurately measuring the properties of quarks and gluons in a variety of collision scenarios. Thanks to advances in natural language processing, generating precise natural language is now possible, but interpreting this generated output into structured formats like SQL remains a challenge. Current approaches primarily focus on intra-domain tasks, but a more exciting opportunity exists: applying text-to-SQL models across different domains with shared underlying data structures. We introduce a novel auxiliary table prediction task to bridge this domain gap by training the model to predict additional, irrelevant tables. This auxiliary task enhances the ability to incorporate prior knowledge and adapts the model to new environments, leading to improved performance in both intra- and cross-domain settings. We also design a straightforward schema merging technique to facilitate cross-domain applications. Experimentation across various intra- and cross-domain scenarios confirms the effectiveness of our approach. When adapting to a new hotel reservation domain, the model achieves an F1 score 4.5% higher than a baseline, demonstrating its capability to transfer domain expertise. We make our code available at: https://github.com/ghrua/TextToSQL_CrossDomain.

This approach enables the novice student to explore different hypotheses and discover new knowledge. Although primarily developed for self-paced learning, this framework has been adaptable for various applications, both batch and online, due in part to the introduction of the Re-weighing method by the pioneering researcher, which allows for the inclusion of diverse data. This survey delves into the technical aspects of the instructor-student architecture, discusses its applications across various domains, and critically examines its limitations along with potential solutions. Systematic investigations and theoretical analyses have also been conducted to explore the relationship between the instructor and student, which can guide the development of high-performance models. Finally, the paper outlines its own contribution, which includes an original theoretical analysis of the relationship between the instructor and student, along with a novel perspective on the instructor-student architecture as a means of addressing non-convex optimization challenges.
