We investigated the interplay between absorption and a beam of photons in a precise experiment using strontium gas. By analyzing the absorption of a single, high-power laser beam in an ultracold strontium gas, we were able to observe the influence of the recoil of photons on atomic motion. By comparing theoretical predictions to our experimental results, we validated our understanding of this complex interaction and identified a key boundary where the absorption becomes saturated. Furthermore, we accurately measured this boundary and found it to be in close agreement with the results of a simulation that takes photon recoil into account. By scaling our findings for real-world applications, we demonstrated the potential of ultracold gases to serve as precise models for studying light-matter interactions that occur in a wide range of contexts, from atomic absorption to optical cavities and even the creation of Bose-Einstein condensates. By adjusting key variables, we were also able to explore the effects of photon recoil on atomic motion and observed the emergence of a nonlinear relationship between absorption and the intensity of the laser beam. This nonlinearity resulted in a phenomenon known as optical bistability, which we were able to quantify and distinguish from other possible explanations by conducting a series of controlled experiments. Furthermore, our data reveals two distinct shear thickening behaviors that reflect diverse microscopical phenomena, including the interaction between polymer chains and particulate jamming. By applying our findings to real-world scenarios, our research highlights the potential for materials exhibiting this phenomenon to be optimized for a broader range of applications. Lastly, our results underscore the crucial role played by particle interactions at stresses that far exceed those required to initiate the shear thickening transition.

We investigate the capacity of next-generation $e^+e^-$ colliders at TeV energies to detect beyond-Standard Model (BSM) physics through Higgs interactions using Effective Field Theories (EFTs) as a framework. Specifically, we examine double Higgs production within these EFTs and assess the TeV $e^+e^-$ colliders' sensitivity to BSM Higgs interactions at both leading and subleading order in the EFT expansion. Our analysis covers various BSM operators that influence light and heavy Higgs bosons and evaluates the impact of these interactions on collider observables. We calculate the total cross-section for double Higgs production in both leading and subleading orders in the EFT expansion and use these results to determine detectable BSM Higgs interactions at the High Luminosity Large Hadron Collider (HL-LHC), the Future Circular $e^+e^-$-Collider (FCC$e$), and the Compact LInear Collider (CERN) study (CLIC). Our findings demonstrate that the HL-LHC, with a center-of-mass energy of 27.5 TeV and 15,000 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, can constrain certain BSM Higgs interactions affecting the light Higgs boson at masses up to 500 GeV, while the FCC$e$ can detect similar interactions affecting the heavy Higgs boson at masses up to 800 GeV. On the other hand, the CLIC, with a center-of-mass energy of 380.5 GeV and 5,000 fb$^{-1}$ integrated luminosity, can identify BSM Higgs interactions affecting the heavy Higgs boson at masses up to 1.1 TeV. We also explore the impact of these BSM Higgs interactions on the heavy Higgs boson decay into light Higgs bosons and find that the FCC$e$ can detect such decays into three light Higgs bosons at center-of-mass energies above 450 GeV. Our research underlines the significance of $e^+e^-$ colliders in probing BSM Higgs interactions at high energies and highlights the unique discovery potential of the FCC$e$ in this regard. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material saturated with fluid by conducting experiments and numerical simulations. The object's motion was observed to be affected by various factors, including the friction of individual grains, their overall density, and the object's length in relation to its diameter. Our findings showed that the drag experienced by the object depends oppositely on the angle of its movement, with the front experiencing more drag than the back when moving forward but the opposite when side-rolling occurs. We also discovered that the front and back drag experience different forces even when the object is standing still, due to the random arrangement of grains. Notably, the object's ability to move through the granular bed becomes more difficult when its length is similar to its diameter. Our numerical simulations helped clarify the object's motion by highlighting the importance of grain arrangement and the pressure exerted on the front and back of the object. Our study identified two primary resistance forces acting on the object: a constant force related to the pressure it exerts on the surrounding grains and a variable force associated with the friction of individual grains. Our analysis also showed that the object's motion becomes more resistant as its length increases due to the added pressure on the sides. We compared our experimental and numerical findings to previous research on the drag experienced by objects moving through fluid alone and found that the drag experienced in the granular bed is significantly greater. We also discovered that the object's motion becomes more difficult when its speed is high or when it is standing still, due to the increased pressure it exerts on the surrounding grains. Our study identified two distinct regimes of motion: one where the object moves easily through the granular bed and another where it moves slowly due to the increased resistance. Our analysis of the object's speed over time revealed that the object's speed decreases more rapidly in the granular bed than it would in a fluid alone. Our study provides new insights into the drag experienced by objects moving through a layer of granular material saturated with fluid and can be applied to a wide range of natural phenomena and technological innovations. Our research can be applied to the study of sediment transport in rivers and ocean currents as well as the movement of objects through granular materials in industries such as mining and construction. With a well-established understanding of these processes at the tree level, their minute occurrences can subtly reveal beyond-Standard Model physics. Recent findings from the ATLAS collaboration are presented, featuring the rare decay $B_s\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and the CP-violating decay $B^0\to\phi\mu^+\mu^-$, both exhibiting sensitivity to new physics. By combining theoretical and experimental advancements, the probability of these rare occurrences at the LHC has been accurately determined, paving the way for further, more precise investigations. Lepton flavour and CP violation in $B\to K\mu^+\mu^-$ decays have also been examined and found to conform to established patterns, albeit with scope for future analysis to yield more detailed insights. With ongoing efforts to enhance the LHC's data collection and improve theoretical understanding, these findings position the ATLAS experiment at the forefront of rare and CP-violating beauty meson decay research.

Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing structure-preserving discretizations that conserve important features such as positivity, boundedness, and oscillation. Although such schemes typically employ an explicit time-stepping technique, their combination with efficient solvers like the conjugate gradient method is not well understood. This study bridges this gap by examining the application of preconditioned conjugate gradient methods to systems of the form $M\dot{u} = f(u)$, where $M$ represents a diagonal mass matrix. By establishing relationships between the approximate solutions generated by the conjugate gradient method and the true solution, we prove the preservation of a measure of oscillation, which can be any norm induced by a positive definite matrix. In addition, we demonstrate the convergence of the conjugate gradient method when the inner product induced by a positive definite matrix is used, which implies the preservation of a measure of oscillation under the standard conjugate gradient method. Furthermore, we establish and numerically verify the bounds on the maximum and minimum eigenvalues of the mass matrix $M$ as necessary conditions for maintaining the preservation of a measure of oscillation. These results are then extended to the conjugate residual method and GMRES. This includes an investigation of the impact of the degree of freedom on the spatial discretization and the resulting mass matrix $M$ on the measures of oscillation of the approximate solutions generated by the conjugate gradient method. Soft-tissue navigation, a technique that allows surgeons to view relevant patient anatomy during procedures, relies heavily on registering non-rigid volumes obtained from MRI scans. However, accurate registration of these volumes, particularly in areas with limited access, poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we've developed a novel method for registering abdominal organs using a data-driven finite element model. This model leverages information from a limited set of surface points and normal vectors to align the entire organ, even in complex, non-rigid environments. By utilizing a computationally efficient direct solver, the registration process is significantly accelerated, enabling real-time image-guided surgery. Our method has been rigorously tested using both phantom and in vivo data, yielding superior results in comparison to a state-of-the-art surface-based registration technique. Furthermore, we've observed a notable reduction in registration time, with an average of 0.35 seconds required for abdominal organ registration. These findings support the integration of this method into real-time soft-tissue navigation applications. Our approach has also been made publicly available on GitHub. Additionally, we've applied this technique to a case study involving partial nephrectomy, with promising outcomes. Our data and model are available for further research purposes. Determining the flow between two scenes in different views of the same dynamic scene is a fundamental computer vision problem that has numerous practical applications. Although prior research has focused primarily on using metric learning on the pairs of points belonging to the same scene, we propose a novel method that leverages metric learning on pairs of points, one from each scene, with the aim of determining whether they belong to the same dynamic scene or not. By adopting this adversarial approach, we develop a network that produces a score indicating the likelihood of two points belonging to the same dynamic scene while simultaneously learning a feature representation that accurately predicts the point correspondences. Our method, referred to as Adversarial Self-Supervised Scene Flow Estimation, enables self-supervised scene flow estimation without relying on paired data. Our method has been evaluated on the SfM^2 dataset and yields superior results compared to the current state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, we demonstrate its versatility and practical utility by incorporating it into a 3D tracking system, thereby enhancing the system's performance in dynamic scenes. The project is hosted on the GitHub platform at the link https://github.com/ali-ghafoei/Adversarial-Scene-Flow.

Contemporary microservices utilize containerized services for developing and deploying applications at high speed. As the number of services grows, managing permissions across individual containers becomes an escalating challenge. Existing solutions either overgrant broad permissions or are too restrictive, compromising security or efficiency respectively. In response, we present Timeloops, an innovative, self-governing policy learning approach for containerized microservices. The Timeloops framework automatically generates and refines access control policies in response to changes in system calls made by individual containers during operation. By analyzing past system calls and predicting future behavior, the Timeloops framework creates a predictive model that streamlines policy enforcement and minimizes unnecessary permission adjustments. In evaluation tests involving real-world applications, Timeloops reduces average permission overhead by approximately 70% and successfully implements policies with nearly identical efficacy to manual configurations. Timeloops' lightweight, automated design, coupled with its capacity to balance security and efficiency, positions it as a cutting-edge solution for the increasingly prevalent containerized microservices landscape. Timeloops' lightweight, self-governing approach can balance security and efficiency in containerized microservices environments. Timeloops' code is available online at https://github.com/ucy-cyber/timeloops-containers. Additionally, we determine the optimal size of this control domain required to achieve null controllability. Both theoretical and numerical examples are provided to illustrate these results. The dynamics of soccer games mean that critical moments can suddenly become life-or-death affairs, with side-wide counterattacks arising from the slightest mistake.  These situations often arise where the ball is being chased by multiple players in the middle field.  Current soccer agents fall short in such scenarios due to limited exploration and the complexity of the game.  To improve, we've developed a deep reinforcement learning approach that prioritizes bold action selection by creating a value function that differentiates between similar situations based on the potential consequences of conservative versus daring play.  Our method enables the agent to choose between more cautious or riskier actions even when the game is not directly offering a reward for such behavior.  As a result, the agent becomes more aggressive in situations where doing so could regain control of the ball or launch a counterattack.  We've tested and validated our approach on a realistic soccer simulator, and the resulting agent outperforms standard deep reinforcement learning-based approaches on multiple game scenarios.  Our code is available online at https://github.com/alexmilvagni/soccer-deep-qo.

Unfortunately, traditional imaging methods are ill-equipped to utilize high-frequency surface-wave data due to its short duration. In this research, surface-wave data from three locations in Alaska were analyzed, and a signal-inversion approach known as Extended Source Signal Inversion was successfully applied to incorporate this valuable data in seismic imaging. By directly inverting seismic waves rather than derived properties, this method seamlessly integrates full-waveform seismic data for enhanced, more detailed imaging results. We provide a detailed proof of a recent statement regarding the solvability of certain systems of congruences modulo prime powers, specifically those involving Hecke algebra equations and ideal class group relations for an algebraic number theory extension of Q. This proof builds upon the fundamental work of Leopoldt, by establishing the solvability of such systems and establishing connections to the rationality of Dirichlet L-series. Additionally, we offer explicit bounds for the indices of solvability and rationality, thereby expanding on earlier related results due to Michel and Ellenberg. Furthermore, we offer a corrected and simplified proof of a related statement found in an earlier study by the first author. Lastly, we discuss the implications and potential applications of these results to other related problems. This research was inspired by the ideas presented in a lecture by Michel during the 2010 AIM Summer Graduate School on Algebraic Number Theory.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect is particularly evident in historical pandemics, and it has significant implications for public health policies. To better understand the influence of these events and their critical occurrence threshold, we developed a mathematical model that simulates their impact on the spread of a disease within a community. This model, which takes into account both short-distance transmission among closely connected individuals and longer-distance transmission among more distantly connected individuals, reveals that even minimal levels of high-transmission connectivity can significantly accelerate the spread of a disease and may even lead to a much higher epidemic peak and longer recovery period. By analyzing various scenarios, we also found that a higher frequency of these high-transmission connections among closely connected individuals can result in an even more severe and prolonged epidemic. Consequently, this model provides valuable insights that can be applied to mitigate the spread of a disease by targeting these super-spreader events. By focusing on a simple SIR model as an extension, we were able to derive an explicit expression for the peak epidemic size, which reveals that a very high transmission rate of $\lambda\approx 3.44$ is necessary to prevent a large-scale epidemic. This finding has significant implications for the management of public gatherings and the implementation of effective disease control measures.

Transfer learning in deep neural networks enables effective utilization across diverse tasks and datasets. However, the performance of a trained network can deteriorate when it is applied to tasks that are distant from those it was initially trained on. This paper addresses the challenge of adapting a network that has been trained on a source task to succeed in a target task without utilizing labeled data for the target domain. We leverage unsupervised data from a related task that bridges the gap between the source and target tasks and employ a retrieval augmentation approach to fine-tune the network for the target task. We gather three datasets that facilitate evaluation of this approach in different scenarios, ranging from tasks that are identical to completely distinct. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, retrieving data from identical, similar, and diverse related tasks, and show that it yields performance gains in all scenarios, with the most substantial improvements observed when the data is retrieved from similar related tasks. This approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing models without requiring additional parameters, and we show that a straightforward modification can further enhance its performance when the network and the data distribution are similar. Our code is publicly available at: https://github.com/ghru/Retrieval-Augmentation-Pipeline.

In this work, a group G is defined as having a boolean structure if its involutions form a boolean subgroup. We then explore various properties of such groups and establish connections to other boolean-related characteristics. Specifically, we demonstrate that G's boolean structure is equivalent to the conjugacy of its subgroups consisting of pairs of transpositions that commute with each other. This condition in turn is identical to the conjugacy of all 2-subsets of G's elements, which results in G being isomorphic to the symmetric group S8. This specific structure of S8(s) is also shown to be unique by proving that any finite group that has both a boolean structure and 2-transitivity is precisely S8(n). Finally, we examine the implications of a finite group's boolean structure for its irreducible characters and obtain a characterization of its character degrees. This characterization leads to a lower bound on the number of a finite group's irreducible characters when that group has a boolean structure. This in turn enables us to determine the finite groups with the fewest irreducible characters when they have a boolean structure and show that these groups are consistently symmetic groups of the form S8(n). The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision that significantly influences classification performance. While numerous loss functions are available, selecting the most suitable one can be overwhelming due to the diverse options. Recent research introduced a quantitative approach to assess loss function variations' impact by framing it within a mathematical optimization framework. This method evaluates the optimal loss function for a specific classification problem by maximizing the difference between the selected class's probability and that of alternative classes. We investigate three distinct loss functions commonly employed in practice and demonstrate that, under ideal conditions, the optimal loss function yields a probability distribution that accurately reflects the true data distribution. We further develop a scalable algorithm to efficiently estimate the optimal loss function for real-world data by leveraging a stochastic approximation technique. Experimental evaluations on multiple datasets reveal that using the estimated optimal loss function leads to improved classification performance compared to conventional loss functions, as measured by both accuracy and AUC-ROC scores. Moreover, the approach is shown to be robust when the availability of additional data is limited. We also explore the relationship between the estimated optimal loss function and conventional ones and find that, with sufficient data, the estimated optimal loss function converges to a suitable default loss function, such as the softmax cross-entropy loss, which is already widely adopted in practice. We demonstrate and analyze the scalability of the proposed algorithm by applying it to large-scale image classification datasets and show that it can handle over a million training examples on a single GPU. We further discuss the connection to adversarial training and provide a numerical estimate of the optimal loss function variation's scale. Finally, we offer a Python implementation of the proposed algorithm as well as guidelines for selecting hyperparameters. We also discuss and analyze the implications of our results for the design of loss functions for deep learning-based self-play methods, provide numerical evidence regarding the optimal loss function's impact on the robustness of models, and explore its connection to the problem of overfitting. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions along with the code available at: https://github.com/loss-estimation.

Correspondence between geometric and thermodynamic descriptions of gravitating quantum systems relies on the geometric interpretation of temperature in terms of surface gravity, and the volume of spacetime encoded in its holographic boundary. Building upon this framework, we investigate how the quantum capacity and compressibility of an arbitrary, thermally-driven quantum field system are influenced by their inherent properties. Notably, we find that the quantum capacity is directly tied to the entropy density of the system, while the compressibility is linked to its energy density. Consequently, over a wide range of temperatures, the quantum capacity and energy density exhibit a contrasting relationship, with the compressibility displaying a non-monotonic behavior in between. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the geometric interpretation of temperature and the holographic principle collectively ensure that the quantum capacity remains non-negative, even in the presence of a negative energy density. Lastly, we provide specific examples involving free scalar fields in $1+1$ and $3+1$ dimensions to illustrate these findings. By integrating the quantum capacity and compressibility within the geometric and thermodynamic description of spacetime, we can predict its future evolution and assess its stability in both local and global contexts. Moreover, we propose a new, operationally-friendly definition of quantum compressibility that is more amenable to experimental verification. Lastly, we discuss the implications of these results for the Hertel-Buchle protocol, the Hawking effect, and the stability of anti-de Sitter spacetime.

Developing a comprehensive understanding of how machines employ intelligence was long hindered by the absence of a suitable analytical framework. Our research introduces the ATOMIC framework, a systematic tool for dissecting the ins and outs of artificial neural networks by interpreting if-then reasoning. Unlike prior methods that focus on either computational representations or statistical properties, the ATOMIC framework integrates both perspectives to provide a unified and all-encompassing analysis of how machine intelligence functions. By leveraging the ATOMIC framework's features, we demonstrate a tangible example using a simple linear regression, and further showcase its versatility in a more complex setting using a state-of-the-art language model. These examples serve to illustrate the method's capacity to reveal subtle aspects of machine intelligence, ultimately contributing to the development of the ATOMIC framework as a versatile atlas for exploring the intricacies of artificial intelligence. By sharing the ATOMIC framework with the scientific community, we aim to equip researchers with a valuable tool to investigate the intricacies of machine intelligence, paving the way for a deeper understanding of how machines employ their intelligence.

To address this limitation, we focus on modifying the Quantum Linear Systems algorithm to make it suitable for NISQ devices by creating a portfolio of Quantum Linear Systems solving and Monte Carlo sampling. To enhance data efficiency of end-to-end ASR training and facilitate seamless transition to fully sequential decoding, we introduce a novel bidirectional focus method that enables simultaneous multi-modal learning with both sequential decoding and text-based training. Initially, the model focuses on the input sequence by generating the next character, and subsequently, it focuses on the output sequence by predicting the previous character. We link the forward and backward focuses using a shared hidden state, ensuring that the learned representations are consistent and can be exploited for improved ASR performance. Moreover, our approach prevents overfitting by introducing a forward reconstruction loss during backward focus, and we explore various combinations of forward and backward losses to achieve optimal performance. Our proposed method demonstrates superior results in comparison to baseline ASR systems, with a 6.15% relative improvement in WER on the Librispeech corpus. Moreover, we observe an 8.5% reduction in WER when transferring from an all-parallel decoder to a sequential decoder, thereby validating the effectiveness of our approach for seamless transition to fully sequential decoding. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior holds. This result generalizes a prior finding by Diaconis and Hicks, who explored the asymptotic behavior of a single position in $\pi_n$. Lastly, we discuss some connections to a prior result by Batteilino, Hicks, and Sen, who studied the asymptotic behavior of a randomly generated uniform subsequence of the first $k_n$ positive integers. For applications such as video surveillance, object removal, and video editing, predicting a new view of a video from a given perspective is a highly useful capability. In response to these limitations and building on the success of view video prediction methods, we develop a novel algorithm to forecast a new view of a video by leveraging a dual representation framework in conjunction with a spatial and temporal refinement network. In contrast to conventional methods that predict both views and then swap them, our approach eliminates the need to forecast the original view, thereby significantly reducing memory and computational demands. Moreover, our method boasts improved prediction accuracy compared to the conventional approach. We demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of our method on a variety of datasets, including the CMU View Prediction Dataset and the VGGView Dataset, and show it to be a more compact and superior alternative to conventional deep learning-based methods for new view video prediction. In this study, we experimentally verify the effectiveness of inter-level coupling by observing the reduction of quantum coherence between two distinct levels of a system that are not directly connected, based on a solid-state implementation using a nitrogen-vacancy center in a diamond. The successful execution of this method results in a diminished signature of a quantum signature in a density matrix. The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect in Bi/Co multilayers has been investigated by combining first-principles calculations and micromagnetic simulations.  Realizing that strong interface interaction plays a crucial role in these systems, we have employed a method of calculating the effective magnetic interaction by solving the Heisenberg Hamiltonian using first-principles calculations as the interaction term.  This approach has been utilized to determine the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) influence on the magnetic moments and the magnetic anisotropy energy (MAE) in Co layers.  Our calculations have shown that the SOC impact on the magnetic moments and the MAE in the Co layers depends on whether the Bi layers are deposited on top or in contact with the Co layers due to the differing strength of the interface interaction with the substrate.  Furthermore, we have demonstrated that the SOC effect on the magnetic moments and the MAE in the Co layers is influenced by the magnitude of the interface interaction with the substrate.  Our calculated values of the SOC-induced magnetic anisotropy energy per unit cell for a Co layer that is in direct contact with a vacuum layer are 1.35 meV, a value that is comparable to previous experimental and theoretical findings.  Our study has also explored the magnitude of the interface interaction with the substrate by analyzing the SOC-induced magnetic anisotropy energy per unit cell for a Co layer that is in direct contact with a Bi layer, and found that it is 3.5 meV, a value that is greater than expected based on calculations of the SOC effect alone.  To clarify this unexpected result, we have carried out additional calculations to determine the contribution of the interface interaction with the Bi layer to the SOC-induced MAE in the Co layers.  Our analysis has shown that the interface interaction with the Bi layer exerts a direct influence on the magnetic moments and the MAE in the Co layers through the $s-d$ hybridization, and that this effect can be either stabilizing or destabilizing, depending on the magnitude of the interface interaction with the substrate. The potential in question is defined by a specific mathematical structure that includes fractional powers of the Laplace operator. To solve the Schrödinger equation, the potential is transformed using a new scaling parameter, resulting in a series expansion that enables the solution of the equation using the perturbation method. Both bound and scattering states' wave functions are determined by applying the perturbation method and expanding the solution in a series of the scaling parameter. The corresponding energy eigenvalue equations and dispersion relation are also obtained through the same expansion procedure. The study of a harmonic oscillator-like potential, which arises as a specific case of the generalized Mie-type potential, reveals that both its energy eigenvalue and wave function coincide with those of the harmonic oscillator when the fractional parameter vanishes. The same applies to the scattering state of the $n$-dimensional $l$th partial wave of the short-range $\delta$-potential. We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to ensure the network's ability to generalize well and maintain low sensitivity to input data, we propose a training method that optimizes the connection weights to minimize the Lipschitz constant while utilizing stochastic gradient descent. We derive an upper bound for the difference in loss when moving from the original input to an perturbed input, which is dependent on the network's depth, width, and desired level of generalization. We also conduct an empirical study, which demonstrates that our proposed training method to limit the network's sensitivity results in performance comparable to traditional regularization techniques when evaluating the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. We further investigate the proposed method's applicability to deeper networks and find that adding an extra fully connected layer can result in improved performance. We also explore alternative ways to enforce the network's Lipschitz continuity by training the network to detect whether two input samples are identical or not, which yields a model that exhibits robustness to various types of adversarial attacks. We conclude that enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity through regularization results in improved performance when evaluating a range of benchmark datasets.

Quantifying radiation exposure during PET scans is crucial, but it typically results in longer scan times and less accurate data. To compensate for low-dose data, deep learning-based image reconstruction techniques, specifically multimodal learning methods, have shown promise by utilizing both low-dose and standard-dose images for better quality images. However, such models struggle with scans that significantly deviate from typical data patterns. To address these limitations, we developed an uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework that leverages physics-based noise models to enhance the capability of low-dose PET image reconstruction. This approach ensures that the network can effectively utilize both low-dose and standard-dose data, even in situations where the distribution of data may have changed. To evaluate the robustness and performance of this method, we tested it on both in-domain and out-of-domain data, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both cases. Specifically, when comparing the quality of reconstructed images from low-dose data with ground truth standard-dose images, our method produced an SSIM of 0.734 and an FSNR of 10.052 in in-domain settings and an SSIM of 0.683 and an FSNR of 8.151 in out-of-domain settings. These results demonstrate that our method can effectively handle both typical and unusual data distributions, resulting in high-quality PET images with 90% less dose. This approach is now available online for further development and improvement.

We investigate the impact of centering theory on neural coreference resolution within the framework of a general-purpose system. Centering theory, originally developed for analyzing dialogue, positions the "core" or central entity of a sentence as the one with which the focus of conversation remains constant. We examine whether incorporating elements of this theory that are tied to coreference, such as identifying the central referent and tracking referent salience, can improve a state-of-the-art neural coreference resolution system for English. Our experiments involve crafting a salience-aware model by integrating a simple dependency-based method to determine whether a mention is the central referent, along with a learned salience model to rank the referential status of mentions. We also explore a more complex approach using a multi-task learning design to train the system on both salience and centrality estimation simultaneously. Our analysis shows that both of these approaches yield better F-score scores compared to the baseline system but struggle with B^2-accuracy, indicating difficulties with boundary accuracy that persist even when incorporating elements of centering theory. Our findings suggest that while neural coreference resolution systems already excel at capturing the central aspect of centering theory, further work is necessary to enhance their performance in predicting the relationships between mentions within a sentence. We hope this analysis will pave the way for exploring the link between coreference and centering theory in more depth. Our code is available online.

A precise and efficient localization system is crucial for various WiFi applications including smart routing, intrusion detection, and navigation. Traditionally, fingerprinting techniques, which identify locations based on distinct WiFi signal characteristics, have been widely adopted but suffer from significant limitations due to their reliance on extensive initial data collection and calibration processes. Furthermore, their accuracy declines in areas with rapidly evolving wireless environments. In response to these challenges, machine learning-based methods have gained popularity as more agile and adaptive alternatives. In this research, we explore three fundamental aspects of WiFi-based positioning systems through machine learning: whether they should be range estimation or location identification methods, what should be used as input features, and what type of machine learning model is most effective. We tested various combinations of these elements using a carefully curated dataset and found that a specific approach, utilizing K-means clustering to create compact signal profiles and learning the association between learned signal profiles and estimated distances, yields the most accurate range estimation results to date. These findings have significant implications for the design of real-world systems, offering actionable advice for practitioners seeking to deploy similar systems in their own communities. These systems, which provide accurate distance estimates based on reduced dataset collections, are particularly well-suited for applications in urban settings with dense population concentrations. In these environments, the wireless landscape changes rapidly, necessitating a more agile and adaptive localization system like the one proposed here. In addition to these benefits, our research also yields a novel approach to learning the underlying structure of WiFi signal characteristics, a key element missing from the existing literature. In its current form, this approach works well with scatternet structures but also offers the potential for further generalization to more complex configurations. In summary, our solution offers a cutting-edge, universally applicable solution to the challenges of designing a WiFi-based range estimation system. In our experiments, we demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach in both idealized simulation environments and real-world settings, with the resulting system showing significant performance improvements over comparable, widely adopted alternatives. In the course of this research, we also encountered a previously unaddressed challenge related to the validation of our proposed approach, which we resolved by developing a novel simulation-based assessment methodology that provides actionable insights for the broader research community. In its current form, this assessment method is tailored to the specific context of range estimation but also offers the potential for further generalization to a wider range of applications. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved. In an energy recovery linac, where a low-energy particle beam interacts with a high-energy, counter-rotating beam, the influence of beam bunch interaction is more complex and depends on filling patterns. This study investigates how different filling designs impact beam breakup instability and identifies a filling design that minimizes the effect of beam interaction, thus allowing for higher current particle beams. Counter-intuitively, using a counter-rotating beam, rather than a rotating beam, was found to reduce the beam breakup instability, but only in specific filling designs. If an energy recovery linac employs an alternating gradient lattice, research suggests that beam breakup instability can be disregarded due to its minimal impact. However, if a focusing lattice is used instead, there are particular design criteria that must be met in order to manage the beam breakup instability. By exploring various filling patterns, the most effective ones were found to be those with a long gap between particle beam bunch trains, as well as a specific arrangement known as an "odd bunch" filling, which both significantly reduce the beam breakup instability and allow for higher current particle beams. By mitigating the beam breakup instability, the most constrained parameter in an energy recovery linac can be made less restrictive, allowing for a wider range of applications. Given that energy recovery linacs are often used in high-power particle beam applications, such as cancer treatment and advanced accelerator testing, this breakthrough holds considerable value. The findings presented in this study are particularly relevant to the Advanced Proton Treatment Project, a proposed energy recovery linac that requires high current particle beams. By adopting a specific filling design, such as the "odd bunch" arrangement, this project can significantly increase its overall performance. The authors would also like to acknowledge the contributions of Dr. Jerry Staples, a retired SLAC researcher. The study was carried out using the LASER code, a numerical simulation tool specifically designed for energy recovery linac research. The outcomes of this study have been incorporated into the LASER code and will be made available to the scientific community through the APS Physics website. The research presented in this paper was featured at the 2008 Particle Accelerator Conference held in Vancouver, Canada. A new mathematical approach uses a change of variables to convert these complex situations into a similar, easier-to-analyze form in one dimension. We searched archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey for binary and quadruple star systems consisting of two 0.~th magnitude asters.  Asters with positive magnitudes indicate that their brightness exceeds a certain limit, making them difficult to distinguish from stars.  We employed the ADAM algorithm, originally developed for finding specific patterns in the LHC data, to rapidly identify these systems by matching pre-computed models of binary and quadruple star appearances to Pan-STARRS1 images.  Out of 1,200 searched images, we discovered 32 containing two 0.~th magnitude asters with separations ranging from 1.5 to 20.~arcsec and axes of inclination between 30 and 180 degrees.  We determined the orbital periods for these binary systems by analyzing light curves from the APASS, ASAS, and VPHAS survey databases and found that they fall within a narrow range (10 to 30 days) with periods that are nearly commensurate (2.5:1) and light curves that are synchronized with the brighter component.  We also calculated the total system masses and found that they lie within a specific range (0.05 to 0.2 solar masses) with an average of 0.08 solar masses.  We propose a method for converting the light curves of binary aster systems to the HD 209433 equivalent by adjusting the light curve period.  We stress that a deeper understanding of the physics underlying this specific binary aster system is necessary to interpret these results fully. Dungeons and Dragons is a role-playing game that fosters creative problem-solving, social connection, and engaging storytelling. The interplay between players and the Dungeon Master (DM) drives the narrative forward, with the DM using their knowledge of character motivations and psychological insights to guide the story and influence player decisions. By mastering this dynamic, a computer program can excel at various tasks such as creating conversational dialogue and guiding multiple possible story paths. To tackle this challenge, we developed a unique approach that teaches the model to recognize the intents and mental states of players, leveraging a custom-made dataset of D&D conversations. Our approach yields a 12% improvement in accuracy when predicting player actions and a 5% gain in overall conversational coherence. Furthermore, we introduce a novel method to assess the theory-of-mind component by simulating different mental state configurations and evaluating the conversational outcomes. To evaluate the overall conversational experience, we developed a scoring system that combines various aspects of the conversation, including coherence, consistency, and player satisfaction. Ultimately, our approach enables a computer program to assume the role of a Dungeon Master in a solo D&D adventure, resulting in a 25% improvement in overall engagement scores when compared to a randomly generated DM. Our approach, along with the evaluation tools and dataset, are available at the website listed. With these advancements, we believe a computer program can effectively guide multiple possible story paths in a D&D setting, paving the way for exciting applications in areas such as game development, virtual reality, and educational tools. The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional flexibility is highly intriguing and has sparked significant debate. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of various protein structures using advanced topological tools, revealing diverse knotting patterns across different protein families. Our study utilizes magnetic resonance (MR) constraints to pinpoint the precise three-dimensional shapes of six cysteine-free knotted proteins, and applies advanced topological methods to map their complex structures. By tracing specific bond closures around these spatial arrangements, we successfully identify distinct patterns of bond closures associated with each of the protein structures. Notably, our findings reveal that the most prevalent cross-over paths in these knotted proteins consistently bypass specific types of bond closures, which are characterized by particular twisted configurations. When we account for these avoided cross-over patterns in simulated models of the proteins, their natural state configurations demonstrate a significantly reduced occurrence of knotting. Conversely, intentionally forcing these cross-over paths in the simulated models significantly increases the knotting frequency, suggesting that the specific arrangement of bond closures around these proteins plays a crucial role in preventing knotting. Our research highlights the precise mechanisms by which the complex arrangement of bond closures prevents knotting in proteins, providing a detailed understanding of the intricate relationship between protein structure and knotting. Let $\omega$ be a standard symplectic form on the real $n$-dimensional space $ \mathbb{R}^n$. For $n$ being even, we define the $(n,n)$-symplectic mapping category group $ \Lambda_{(n,n)}^{2\pi} ( \mathbb{T}^{2n})_{{\rm reg}}$ as the group generated by the symplectic mapping class groups of symplectic blowups of $ ( \mathbb{R}^{2n}, \omega) / \mathbb{Z}^{n}$ up to isotopy. When $n$ is odd, we consider the $(n,n+2)$-symplectic mapping class group $ \Lambda_{(n,n+2)}^{2\pi} ( \mathbb{T}^{2n+2})_{{\rm reg}}$ defined in a similar manner. Both of these groups form a category whose objects are the blowups of $ ( \mathbb{R}^{2n}, \omega) / \mathbb{Z}^{n}$ and morphisms are generated by ramified cover mappings induced by the standard one-parameter group of rescalings in symplectic geometry. By identifying isomorphism classes of blowups, we establish that the mapping category group for both the even and odd dimensional cases is generated by the monoid consisting of positive integers divided by their greatest common divisor, and includes a subgroup generated by the Seifert surfaces of degree two maps. Furthermore, we show that the mapping category group for both the even and odd dimensional cases is isomorphic to the quotient of its integral version by its torsion elements, which is then isomorphic to the ring of integers divided by their greatest common divisor. Lastly, we establish that the integral version of the mapping category group for both the even and odd dimensional cases is topologically generated by the countable set consisting of positive integers.

A detailed investigation of a specific type of symmetry breaking, known as time-reversal or CP symmetry breaking, is conducted to understand the associated Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem within the context of both relativistic and non-relativistic quantum field theories. A particular time-reversal symmetry breaking scenario, characterized by the presence of a single massless fermionic NG boson and a set of massive scalar NG bosons, in both its real and complex forms, is explored through a comprehensive analysis of its impact on the theory's perturbative stability. The effects of symmetry breaking on the NG spectrum are then examined by perturbing the theory using a small symmetry-breaking parameter. The application of the $C$-operator technique allows for the identification of the NG fields and the derivation of a modified pole equation that includes the influence of the perturbing coupling. The resulting expression for the NG pole function is systematically constructed by employing both the $\epsilon$-regularization and $\Pi$-regularization methods. The analysis reveals that the presence of the perturbing coupling generates a term that violates the causality principle and leads to the creation of a scalar NG boson from the vacuum radiation, when the time-reversal symmetry breaking is achieved through the interaction with a fermionic NG boson. The connection between this phenomenon and the Jona-Lasinio model is also established. The study concludes by discussing its implications on the stability of the QCD theory and the associated vacuum radiation effects. The approach employed in this research can be applied to other time-reversal or CP-symmetry breaking scenarios, offering a valuable framework for exploring the associated NG theorem in a wide range of quantum field theories. The comprehensive analysis presented in this paper provides a detailed understanding of the time-reversal or CP-symmetry breaking NG theorem and its associated consequences, with possible connections to open problems in high-energy particle physics. The study offers a solution to the mystery posed by the original author in 1989 regarding the absence of the $\pi^{0}$ meson in the spectrum of NG bosons in the $\mathcal{P}$ or $\mathcal{T}$-symmetry broken theories and explains the associated vacuum radiation effects in the QCD theory. The research also resolves the second unresolved issue raised in 1992, regarding the failure to identify the correct pole equation for the NG boson field in the presence of the perturbing coupling. In our analysis, we interpret large language models as generating specific types of phrasal counterfactuals. We propose a novel assessment metric called Factual Acceptance, which gauges the ability of these models to reject counterfactuals that describe factual scenes. We discover a significant discrepancy between the performance of models in rejecting counterfactuals about specific entities and those involving general categories. To bridge this gap, we develop a dataset comprising 13,000 counterfactual phrases related to various entities and categories. We utilize this dataset to fine-tune a set of pre-existing conditioning techniques, thereby enhancing the performance of our BART-based model in accurately identifying genuine and fabricated counterfactual phrases. By leveraging these techniques, we create a model capable of generating specific, plausible counterfactual phrases. We refer to this model as DISCO. When combined with existing world models, we find that counterfactual conditionals formed using DISCO improve the accuracy of our previous best-performing approach by approximately 5%. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these counterfactual phrases can be employed to accurately determine whether specific entities or categories are real or fabricated. When combined with an active learning strategy, we achieve an approximately 10% improvement in our previous best-performing approach. Lastly, we explore the potential of these counterfactual phrases to enhance the performance of our BART-based model, finding that training on counterfactual phrases related to specific entities boosts the model's accuracy by approximately 3%. On the other hand, training on counterfactual phrases related to general categories results in a decrease in performance. We believe that our findings have significant implications for the evaluation and training of large language models. We have made our code and datasets publicly available on GitHub. Research into remote epitaxy holds considerable promise, with the potential to minimize material waste and facilitate the creation of complex, thin-film materials with desired properties. This technique, which allows films to be grown at a site distant from their substrate, could be made efficient with the use of graphene as a substrate due to its minimal interaction with growing films. However, achieving controlled epitaxy on graphene requires a precise understanding of the interface between the film, graphene, and vacuum. In this study, we investigated the remote epitaxy of Heusler films on graphene substrates using low-energy electron diffraction and scanning transmission electron microscopy. Our findings reveal that the films exhibit a mixed phase structure consisting of both faceted islands and level layers, and that increasing deposition rates accelerates the transition from a faceted phase to a level phase. Furthermore, we identified that the faceted phase is likely the result of a competition between island coalescence and the formation of holes in existing islands, and that this can be controlled by adjusting deposition rates to prevent island coalescence and level layers to form in previously deposited islands, thereby promoting the growth of level layers. Our results also demonstrate that it's possible to grow level layers on graphene even at low deposition rates, and that further increasing deposition rates results in the formation of small holes in level layers, ultimately transitioning to a van der Waals epitaxy phase. Our study highlights the intricacies involved in Heusler film growth on graphene and the importance of controlling deposition rates to achieve desired outcomes. Our findings are relevant to the development of Heusler-based materials and provide a starting point for further research into this field. Our approach, which combines experimental and theoretical analysis, can also be applied to the study of other thin-film materials. Our results demonstrate that it is possible to achieve controlled epitaxy through the deposition rate, and that this can be achieved without the use of graphene substrates, providing an alternative method for developing complex thin-film materials with desired properties. In this context, where the category of observables is taken as a fundamental starting point, the associated states can be seen as derived quantities. We provide a theoretical framework to recover the original state from its corresponding observable. This involves using a 2-categorical dual of the concept of pullback, which helps in obtaining the 2-vector (functorial) representation of an observable state. This process is analogous to calculating the pullback of a state's representation in a classical context. We demonstrate this concept using both finite-dimensional systems and infinite-dimensional systems, including those represented by operator algebras. This approach leads to a more general and refined understanding of the relationship between categories of observables and associated states. It also provides a foundation for exploring additional physical principles, such as symmetries and unitarity, by incorporating them into the category of observables. Such environments are prone to various types of interference and distortion that can be present due to recording methods, background noise, and the inherent properties of cardiac sounds. In response to these challenges, this study investigates how cardiac sound feature extraction methods are affected by two types of real-world distortions commonly encountered in practice. The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices enables continuous health monitoring for individuals. However, the geographical dispersion and security concerns surrounding these mobile devices limit their capacity for centralized data analysis. To address this challenge, we propose FedHealth, a federated transfer knowledge framework that facilitates real-time, decentralized, and secure health assessment using mobile devices. By leveraging a locally optimized model and coordinating with the cloud server, FedHealth showcases precisely how a mobile device can leverage a global model without accessing raw data and utilize local data to contribute to the global model without revealing sensitive information. We further provide a locally optimized model selection framework and a coordinated algorithm to ensure that the model meets predetermined health standards across various devices. Experimental evaluations conducted on a realistic dataset obtained from wearable ECG recordings reveal that FedHealth yields notable improvements in accuracy and reduces loss when compared to non-transfer and non-coordinated methods. The adaptable FedHealth framework is applicable to various wearable healthcare scenarios, paving the way for its utilization in real-world, large-scale healthcare applications. The code for FedHealth is available online at: https://github.com/gholooi/FedHealth.

If future PTA data achieve a similar level of precision, then eccentric signals from individual binaries may exhibit specific persistent signatures in the timing residuals over a timespan of approximately 10 to the power of 5 years. If verified, this would signify a major breakthrough in the direct detection of individual binary black hole mergers and effectively link two different approaches for detecting gravitational waves. Lastly, implementing this analytical method in our analysis resulted in detection thresholds one order of magnitude more stringent than previously anticipated, primarily due to the incorporation of accurate solutions for general relativity that are specifically tailored to the specific parameters of eccentric binaries in their inspiral phase. Consequently, future research aimed at identifying these PTA signals in actual data using the GWPhasing code should focus on employing the analytical approach discussed in this paper.

We have theoretically analyzed various methods for converting spinless atoms into molecules via three-body recombination. It is crucial to develop such a method as it could be a crucial step in achieving universal quantum gates with which trapped neutral atoms are equipped. Leveraging an example with which we are familiar, consisting of $^{87}$Rb atoms, we have determined the necessary conditions to achieve a high efficiency of spinor atom-molecule conversion. By utilizing a combination of coaxial beams to provide sufficient overlap between the recombination region and the detection zone, we have found that it is possible to achieve a high rate of atom-molecule conversion while minimizing the formation of two atoms per three-body recombination event. Furthermore, we have calculated the optimal beam intensity and position to maximize the molecule-atom recombination rate to approximately 10 times the three-body recombination rate observed in similar conditions. By implementing an atom-molecule conversion process based on two-beam configurations, with one beam inducing three-body recombination and the another beam detecting the molecule, we have determined that it is possible to achieve a rate of atom-molecule conversion as high as $10^4$ times the three-body recombination rate. By successfully developing this atom-molecule conversion technique, it could be applied to various other spinor atom-molecule conversion systems with which it is similar.

In this work, we build upon Strickert et al.'s decoding algorithm and enhance its efficiency by a significant factor, specifically by reducing the required resequencing effort from exponential to polynomial in response to data updates, and simplifying the decoding hierarchy from exponential to linear. This research involves comparing the efficiency of various solvers used to solve linear systems arising from the finite element method in biophysical heart cell modeling. We examined 3 popular solvers using algebraic multigrid methods and 2 strategies employing multilevel preconditioners with a Krylov method, assessing their performance on different computer architectures and modeling time scales. Our investigation included studying the impact of key modeling variables such as membrane conductance and electrical stimulation. We observed that the multilevel preconditioned CG solver offered the best results, with a significant improvement when employing an optimized version of the Finite Element Algebraic Multigrid solver. Furthermore, we found that directly solving the nonlinear heart cell equations numerically can be a viable alternative for certain scenarios. Our findings have implications for both large-scale biophysically detailed modeling and mathematical reductionist approaches to studying heart cell function. They also highlight the importance of carefully selecting solvers and models to match the specific problem being investigated. Our validated code is available online for further research applications.

For large-scale datasets with constant growth, maintaining performance through lifelong reinforcement learning is crucial.
Multiple evaluation environments are proposed to facilitate meaningful assessments of lifelong learning methods.
We introduce L2Explorer, a groundbreaking evaluation framework that comprises nine diverse, increasingly difficult lifelong learning scenarios.
Each scenario is carefully designed to assess different facets of lifelong learning, from steady progress to precise knowledge retrieval.
L2Explorer enables precise measurement of various lifelong learning qualities, including the ability to adapt, avoid forgetting, and achieve steady progress.
By leveraging a modular design, potential new evaluation tasks can be easily integrated into the framework.
We outline specific guidelines for developing custom evaluation protocols within L2Explorer.
By utilizing a cloud-based platform for effortless management and minimal setup costs, L2Explorer streamlines the evaluation process and eliminates the need for repeated data collection.
We also provide detailed implementation details, code, and access to the platform to facilitate widespread use and further development of the framework.
L2Explorer is an open-source platform available at https://l2explorer.com/.

Business Process Discovery aims to create a detailed process model from incomplete and potentially inaccurate data about an organization's practices. The available information typically takes the form of event logs containing partially and inaccurately reported processes. To overcome these limitations, we developed a method to analyze process models using audit logs that may contain incomplete or misleading information about declarative processes. Declarative processes are defined by restrictions on the allowed states of processes rather than step-by-step procedures. We tested our approach on synthetic data and real-world data from a hospital appointment process. The results show that our method can effectively identify processes even with incomplete information and accurately represents processes from hospital appointment data with a low number of incorrect processes. The approach and empirical testing are presented in this paper. Controlling for factors such as galaxy type, redshift, and luminosity distance, we find that the enhanced SFRs in massive galaxies without nuclei can be explained by the presence of a supermassive black hole, which regulates star formation through feedback from the central bulge. X-ray images contain subtle changes that indicate a patient's severity of lung disease.  As a result, images can be utilized for both diagnosis and assessing disease progression.  In intensive care units (ICUs), patients with respiratory conditions are closely monitored to determine if life-support measures are required. Decisions of this nature heavily rely on the assessment of their condition. In this paper, we explore the concept of using image features to make inferences about a patient's ICU admission potential due to severe lung disease. To achieve this, we gathered a large dataset of x-ray images featuring various lung conditions. Next, we applied a set of feature extraction techniques to obtain a compact set of image attributes. These attributes were then utilized to train a machine learning model to predict ICU admission potential for each new image. To validate our approach, we conducted a series of experiments using cross-fold training to ensure the accuracy of our findings. The results showed a significant improvement in predicting ICU admission potential with a combination of our proposed features. Moreover, the findings were applicable across different machine learning models tested. To further analyze the findings, we conducted a feature importance analysis to identify the key image attributes contributing to accurate predictions. The key contributions of this research are (1) the introduction of a novel concept, i.e., predicting ICU admission potential from x-ray images, (2) an enlarged public dataset of x-ray images featuring various lung conditions, and (3) a set of features and a machine learning model capable of accurately predicting ICU admission potential from x-ray images. The proposed approach has the potential to be integrated into clinical decision support systems, thus enhancing the effectiveness of medical diagnoses. Classifying visual relationships using images has a significant issue: the vast majority of training data are incorrect, where the subject, object, or relationship is misidentified. We call these "difficult positive data." Since the majority of the data are normal, standard resampling methods are ineffective due to the majority class overwhelming the minority. We propose a new algorithm, Spatial Mix Ratio, to address this imbalance by variably blending class proportions based on spatial object dependencies. We find this method enhances the performance of state-of-the-art models by 3.3% on the Visual Relationship Detection dataset. By further integrating hard negative mining and a relation-aware linear transformation, our proposed method achieves superior results, surpassing existing records by 5.3%. Code is available at https://github.com/zhengyangyao/Spatial-Mix-Ratio-VRD.

Recently discovered solar observations from Bolivia (5250 m above sea level) and Mexico (4600 m above sea level) uncovered a significant air shower event resulting from neutrons that had decayed in the atmosphere during a powerful X2.0 solar flare on November 7, 2004. Utilizing radio detectors in Mexico (1600 m above sea level) and Bolivia (5200 m above sea level), along with an all-sky camera in Mexico, we identified the shower front and estimated the shower's arrival time, allowing us to calculate the time when the neutrons had decayed in the atmosphere. By correlating this information with solar data, we established that the shower occurred when the Earth's magnetic field was perpendicular to the solar flare's direction, thereby confirming that the neutrons originated from the Sun. Noting that the detected energy fell within the range of 10^12 to 10^13.5 ergs, we calculated the solar neutron flux to be approximately 1.1 x 10^7 neutrons per square centimeter over the atmosphere, with an estimated cosmic ray proton energy spectrum index of 2.7. Furthermore, we estimated the solar electron flux to be 10^9 times greater than the neutron flux, which is consistent with satellite data. Additionally, we calculated the time when the neutrons reached the Earth's surface to be 3.5 minutes after the solar flare, which is consistent with previous findings and suggests that high-energy solar neutrons take this long to arrive on Earth's surface. Lastly, we determined the solar flare's effective area to be approximately 10^-5 steradians, which is a fraction of the total solar surface visible to the Earth, and deduced that the energy of the solar flare was sufficient to produce 10^25 neutrons over the course of a few minutes. In 2011, extraordinary brightness variations were observed on the surface of the young, rapidly rotating A-type star AI Phil (also known as HD 73534). Over the next decade, similar patterns repeated with changing intensity, suggesting an entanglement of stellar rotation and convection influenced by a mysterious outer boundary layer. We used the RAD McGraw method to analyze the surface integral of the mean squared solar-like oscillation amplitude, and found that the convective envelope's angular velocity is synchronized with the 11.631 day rotation period, which is also matched by the 11.631 day duration of a particular p-mode oscillation power hump. We discovered that the p-mode power hump's amplitude is reduced by about 30% compared to expectations, which we attribute to shearing of the power hump due to differential rotation. We estimated the outer boundary layer's thickness and found it to be about 0.035 the radius of the star, which is consistent with the expected thickness based on AI Phil's convective properties. We also determined the star's seismic parameters and found that its mean density is 2.55 plus or minus 0.15 the solar density, which is consistent with the expected mass range of 1.5 to 2.5 solar masses. We calculated the star's mean luminosity and temperature, which are also consistent with the expected values. We considered two possible explanations for the reduced power hump amplitude: a ring of destroyed convective core or an outer boundary layer with a specific angular momentum that's greater than the convective envelope's. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm. Although machine learning models have been successful in identifying false information, especially when there is an abundance of labeled data available, their effectiveness greatly diminishes when they are applied to emerging false news stories. To address this challenge, we present a Meta Neural Process Networks approach that can efficiently detect false news emerging on the scene. This model leverages the idea that it can learn general information about false news and combines this with specific information from a single data point to accurately perform the task. We evaluate our proposed method on a realistic dataset that simulates real-world conditions and find that it significantly outperforms existing baselines in multiple settings. Moreover, our proposed method demonstrates superior performance when compared to a state-of-the-art anti-fake news model that was specifically trained on the same dataset. We also conduct an ablation analysis to understand the contribution of various components of our proposed method and identify several possible ways to improve our model, including integrating external knowledge to enhance its performance. We make our code and dataset publicly available on GitHub. Complex systems comprising interconnected components often follow nonlinear dynamics and exhibit multifaceted behavior. Current methods of nonlinear dynamics learning are typically developed for single-element systems and are not directly applicable to network dynamics. We demonstrate and evaluate our method on both single-element and network systems using graph neural networks.  Our results indicate that learning the dynamics of individual components allows us to generalize to network-level dynamics, and we also explore the impact of various network configurations on our method's effectiveness. This formula has an intriguing dual formulation that can be expressed in terms of the generating functions for the number of partitions satisfying certain congruence properties. Notably, one of these generating functions converges beyond its initial radius of convergence due to a surprising application of Waring's formula, a result originally proved using the circle method. We further explore implications for the original coefficient in homotopy theory and provide a bound on the number of summands required to achieve a specific positive integer, which has a direct interpretation within the context of the topological space $S^n$. Additionally, we establish upper and lower bounds on this number, which can be tightened under the Riemann hypothesis. As a side remark, we establish an unproven conjecture regarding the distribution of the number of summands in a particular partitioning scheme, which may be supported by numerical data but lacks a theoretical explanation. We believe this conjecture holds statistical significance and could potentially have broader implications for the circle method and its applications in number theory. To facilitate verification of the conjecture, we have made available the numerical data underlying it. We also explore connections to earlier results on the integrality of specific coefficients and provide a new proof for an earlier stated formula, which can be further generalized to provide a more comprehensive framework for analyzing similar problems in the field of homotopy theory. We believe this generalization may offer a valuable tool for tackling a broader range of related problems and challenges. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in a dense model with a small number of categories being eliminated, which may limit its practical utility. In response, we develop a modified Group Lasso approach that produces sparse solutions comparable to the Lasso for continuous data by applying an $\ell_\infty$-norm penalty to each group of categories. This strategy enables a degree of within-group sparsity, enhancing the potential for meaningful variable selection and interpretation. We establish theoretical guarantees for our method's performance and validate its practical effectiveness through numerical experiments. The code is publicly available as mlasp.

We create an original proposal to generate the entanglement between two unconnected atoms via Jaynes-Cummings systems, both located in separate environments. By leveraging the semantic meaning of subtitles, a network is designed to accurately determine both the horizontal and vertical angles of the preferred viewpoint. A locally precise approach using conserved quantities in a 1D Heisenberg chain is presented as a precise method for thermal states and time evolution, eliminating the need for approximations and bond dimension. This approach takes advantage of the fact that local operators can accurately capture the long-range behavior associated with conserved quantities. As a result, the network's structure consists solely of 2x2 tensors in the middle section, and approximations are only necessary in the outer regions. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated by comparing it to the local bond dimension method and showing that, with a much smaller bond dimension, the locally precise method achieves the same level of accuracy. This method can also be applied to other models with a conserved Hamiltonian, and it provides a precise and efficient way to describe open quantum systems with long-range interactions. This approach can be implemented using the TNMEP library. Using reinforcement learning to train neural machine translation models has shown promise, but its efficacy is greatly hampered by the vast number of possible translations.  This issue makes learning extremely difficult, but our proposed solution, ActionDecay, efficiently tackles this problem by dynamically reducing the search space based on the relevance of words to the target sentence.  Our results demonstrate that ActionDecay leads to significant improvements in performance, surpassing current state-of-the-art methods in several benchmarks.  We also find that incorporating a decoder's confidence about the target sentence's fluency further enhances the translated text's quality.  Our approach and data are available open-source on GitHub.  With 16 GP106 GPUs, we achieved outstanding translation speed, attaining 5.4 nucleic sentences per second on the WMT'14 English-to-German benchmark.  Our proposed method ranks 6th among 63 submitted papers to the WMT'19 Test Suite.  Our proposed method's simplicity allows it to be combined with other techniques, and our data reveal that combining ActionDecay with the reinforcement learning technique "Monolingual Backtranslation" leads to significant gains in performance.  Our proposed method can be applied to other machine learning tasks involving large action spaces.  We propose a straightforward approach to evaluate the effectiveness of ActionDecay, and our results demonstrate that ActionDecay efficiently finds the most relevant words within a search space.  We also propose a data-driven method to determine the optimal threshold for discarding infrequent words, and our results demonstrate that ActionDecay's performance varies minimally with different threshold values.  We believe our proposed method and results have implications for other machine learning tasks involving large action spaces.  Our code is available open-source on GitHub at the URL https://github.com/ruishanwu/RL-NMT.
