We conduct an in-depth analysis of the nonconvex matrix decomposition problem from a Riemannian perspective, classifying the landscape of fixed-rank matrix optimization tasks as geodesically convex. We demonstrate that matrix factorization problems, including those involving overlapping factors and matrix mean square root decomposition, adhere to this geodesically convex classification. Overlapping factorization matrix optimization is proven to possess a unique minimizer at the bisection point, whereas matrix factorization and mean square root decomposition have convex geodesics within their support sets. Notably, the set defined by the trace norm constraints exhibits geodesic convexity, a property that has never been established before. We further explore the implications of geodesic convexity, showing that it leads to the global convergence and correctness of an iterative reweighting algorithm used for matrix completion and robust matrix factorization. We also analyze the stability of the unique minimizer existing in overlapping factorization cases and prove that it is finite and directly related to the smallest non-zero eigenvalue of the Gramian matrix constructed from the shared columns. Moreover, we establish that the optimal solution to matrix sum-of-squares decomposition problems is characterized by a single hyperplane defined by the inner product of the matrix and its conjugate, which further implies that the Riemannian gradient descent algorithm used is globally convergent along this defined hyperplane. We numerically verify the presence of geodesic convexity through a visualization of the level sets constructed from the distance function along the geodesics within the Grassmannian manifold. We also compare the performance of the reweighting algorithm used for matrix completion and robust matrix factorization on real-world datasets, demonstrating its superior performance to baseline methods used for solving these problems. We conclude by outlining potential future research directions related to fixed-rank matrix optimization, including the analysis of the convexity of the level sets defined by the distance function along the geodesics within the Euclidean space and the development of efficient implementations of the Riemannian gradient descent algorithm used within the Grassmannian manifold. We provide a Python code for reproducing the numerical experiments conducted as part of this research. Before using CNNs in safety-critical systems, it's essential to establish a case for their reliability in the presence of hardware errors. Previous studies on CNNs with faults have focused on training robust models or detecting errors, but have not explored the feasibility of using production-grade CNNs in a fault-tolerant manner. In contrast, this research explores the use of a resilient approach that allows the use of pre-trained, production-grade CNNs without retraining, which reduces deployment costs and minimizes the burden on memory and computational resources. We introduce a novel method to automatically identify a language-independent knowledge base by grouping words with the same semantic in different languages.  Word2Vec's cluster-consistent word embedding generation method allows non-overlapping semantic groups to be distinguished by analyzing variations in embedding space.  We leverage this property to develop a technique for categorizing words into distinct clusters that represent independent semantical meanings.  An evaluation of our approach demonstrates that it effectively differentiates between internal and external cluster semantics.  By utilizing this capability, we gather a set of words that represent each language's unique semantics, which we refer to as the "foreign base."  Subsequent experiments reveal that combining a language's own semantic base with the foreign base incorporated through embedding results in a more accurate classification performance compared to using the embedded representation alone.  Additionally, we found that using the foreign base in the same manner improves classification accuracy when the feature space exceeds two dimensions.  Finally, we explored the applicability of our method to distinguish between different semantic groups within the same language, and found that it can effectively do so, thereby enabling the construction of a multi-lingual common semantic area with varying cluster sizes.  All code and data used in this research are available online.  Sourcing the data from Wikipedia articles, we generated a 1 million-word corpus spanning English, French, Spanish, and Chinese.  Further analysis of this corpus involved developing a protocol to evaluate embedding representation's ability to capture internal and external semantic groupings, as well as investigating the impact of varying cluster sizes and multi-lingual knowledge bases on classification performance.  The resulting findings provide actionable insights for developing more sophisticated multilingual models. This paper presents the production of pions, kaons, protons, and $\phi$ mesons in Xe-Xe collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV. These measurements were conducted by the ALICE collaboration and encompass a wide range of transverse momentum from 0.3 to 8 GeV for pions and kaons, 0.4 to 5 GeV for protons, and 2 to 4.5 GeV for $\phi$ mesons across a range of centrality levels in heavy-ion collisions. Compared to Pb-Pb collisions at a similar centrality, we observe a lead nucleus mass scaling for the averaged number of charged particles and the initial temperature of the system, based on particle ratios. Furthermore, we derive the elliptic flow coefficient ($v_2$) for all measured particles and centrality levels, finding that it is proportional to the number of participating nucleons for a given impact parameter. Additionally, we calculate the radial flow velocity for each particle and find that it is similar across different masses. Finally, using hydrodynamic models, we compare our measurements to heavy-ion collision theory. These findings are significant because they provide a detailed understanding of heavy-ion collisions and offer valuable input for heavy-ion collision theory. Moreover, due to the similarities in detector technology between the ALICE and CBM experiments, these results are also relevant for future heavy-ion collision experiments at the FAIR facility in Germany. Finally, they highlight the importance of heavy-ion collision experiments at the LHC and future facilities like the CBM experiment at the FAIR facility in Germany in advancing our knowledge of heavy-ion collision theory.

In late October 2019, student-led protests erupted in Chile, resulting in extensive civil unrest and nationwide consequences. This study aims to adapt a mathematical model originally developed to describe university student behavior during an influenza outbreak to capture the key features observed throughout the Chilean protests. The model accounts for non-local random connections between individuals, incorporates the impact of external factors similar to influenza transmission rates, and includes a critical mass of students necessary to initiate widespread protest behavior. By applying these assumptions, we derive a mathematical equation representing the development and halt of the protests. Our analysis reveals that the model can replicate the sudden onset, extensive spread, and eventual decline in protests observed in Chile's scenario. Furthermore, we discovered that reducing funding for public education could lead to protests breaking out in a more widespread and intense manner. These findings support the notion that reduced public university financing contributed to the protests' escalation. Additionally, we found that protests are more likely to commence on a larger scale during the winter semester, consistent with empirical data. It has been demonstrated that this approach is applicable to a wide range of scenarios, including some instances where the original method failed, in particular, scenarios with nested regular expressions. It has also been found that, under certain conditions, solving constraints defined by extended regular expressions can be equivalent to solving constraints defined by regular expressions with variables, which provides a more general solution to some specific problems. Mobile devices have limited storage for maps and compass applications but possess high-capacity image and accelerometer sensors. Leverage can be taken of these sensors to enhance the accuracy of compass applications on a small-scale device. Inertial and vision data complement each other as they provide positional information in 3D dimensions and 2D planes respectively. This paper presents a novel external memory attention model, VIO, that employs both visual and inertial data for localization on a small-scale device. The model's ability to process large amounts of visual data is enhanced by an external memory mechanism that prioritizes relevant information. VIO is tested using a custom-made dataset with both linear and rotational movements and yields accurate results compared to a baseline model. The model's efficiency in processing limited map data is proven through an additional experiment where it successfully navigates an unknown environment with a pre-trained map. VIO's code has been made publicly available on the website.

Quantum mechanics relies heavily on linear algebra due to the nature of wave functions and tensors in various physical scenarios. As a result, the concept of dimensionality gained a specific meaning, directly tied to the spatial attributes of linear surfaces in a three-dimensional space. These definitions have been successfully applied across topological phases, surface states, and emitters' interactions. Nonetheless, a generalization of these concepts beyond linear algebra has been achieved by introducing the Weyl semimetal model, which exhibits non-linear, two-joint surfaces defined by cubic equations. By further expanding this framework, we now propose a novel theoretical model - the square-root Weyl material, which is characterized by linear relationships between energy levels and spatial coordinates and exhibits unique topological properties that could be distinguished in experiments using scattering matrices of emitters. Our proposed model can be realized using a combination of square-root operator constructions and provides a theoretical explanation for specific phenomena observed in graphene and other two-dimensional materials. Our study also reveals that the Phases of interface states in the square-root Weyl material are interchangeable with those of the parent Weyl semimetal, thereby offering a controlled environment to examine the impact of linear or non-linear dimensionality on topological phases. Our proposed square-root Weyl material model offers an enriching generalization of the Weyl semimetal framework that can be applied across open systems, two-dimensional materials and three-dimensional systems with a curved surface. This paper presents a numerical solution to the non-compact electromagnetic data completion problem formulated using the quasi-reversibility method. Unlike the compact case where uniqueness of solution holds, without additional constraints, the existence and uniqueness of the solution to the non-compact problem are not guaranteed due to the presence of singular functions in the solution space. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that a specific numerical method can provide an approximate solution to the non-compact problem. By employing a finite element approach and direct solver, we develop a numerical scheme that produces an approximate solution to the original problem. We also leverage a priori regularization theory to establish the convergence of the numerical solutions as the mesh size tends to zero. Furthermore, we show that with suitable time-dependent constraints, we can recover unique solutions and achieve a $\sqrt{\epsilon}$-rate of convergence, where $\epsilon$ represents the strength of the singularities in the solution space. Numerical examples are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of this approach in recovering clean and distorted images and the impact of varying mesh sizes and time-dependent constraints on the solutions. We also explore a more efficient implementation using a preconditioned conjugate gradient method. The numerical solution and associated error estimates are compared to the results obtained using the Bayesian approach proposed in [B. Wei and H. Ammari, Inverse Problems, Vol. 34, 2020]. In the knowledge amalgamation framework, multiple reliable sources provide data with different attributes, and the goal is to combine them into a unified table with a predetermined set of columns. To achieve this, previous methods rely heavily on user input to identify the corresponding columns across sources. However, these approaches overlook the potential benefits of existing data that can guide the amalgamation process. This paper introduces FedMatch, a novel approach that leverages matching data to facilitate the amalgamation process. FedMatch employs a hybrid approach that combines machine learning-based matching with federated learning to achieve this goal. In the initial round, each party trains a machine learning model to automatically match their data with that provided by one reference party. Thereafter, FedMatch enters a phase where model parameters are updated through federated learning, with the objective of maximizing overlap between parties' data. To achieve this, FedMatch incorporates a metric that measures data overlap as a key component in the optimization problem. By solving this problem, the parties collaboratively determine a subset of rows and columns from the combined table that best captures their shared data. Experiments conducted on real and synthetic datasets reveal that FedMatch yields superior results when compared to existing approaches that rely heavily on user input. Moreover, FedMatch demonstrates a high degree of adaptability when confronted with unfamiliar data, as it is capable of expanding its knowledge gradually. This capability enables FedMatch to successfully combine data even in scenarios where matching data is scarce. Finally, FedMatch offers substantial improvements in terms of row and column inclusion when compared to existing methods. To facilitate scalable implementation, FedMatch is designed to operate with a reduced number of communication rounds, a feature that becomes particularly beneficial in presence of limited network connectivity. This is achieved through a combination of batch processing and a communication-efficient federated learning protocol. As a result, FedMatch exhibits a linear relationship between the number of data samples and communication cost. We conducted an in-depth photometric and spectroscopic analysis of the Type II supernova SN 2020jfo, which exhibited a rare and brief luminosity plateau phase, lasting only 13 days. This occurrence is uncommon for its type, as typical SNe II have plateau durations ranging from 30 to 90 days. By matching SN 2020jfo's spectral features to previously observed SNe II spectra, we identified it as a hybrid of SN 1970G and SN 1987A in its early stages, and later as a match for SN 1987A with similar spectral characteristics. The analysis of its $g$-band light curve also revealed a close match to SN 1987A, with SN 2020jfo exhibiting a peak luminosity 0.5 magnitudes brighter than SN 1987A. By utilizing the relationship between the $^{57}$Ni mass and the light curve shape, we estimated the mass of $^{57}$Co in SN 2020jfo to be 0.161 solar masses, and the total $^{57}$Ni mass to be 0.094 solar masses based on the light curve analysis. Conversely, we calculated the $^{57}$Ni mass directly from the nebular phase spectra, obtaining a mass of 0.085 solar masses. The analysis of SN 2020jfo's light curve and the $^{56}$Ni mass distribution also support the theory that it resulted from a massive, rotating progenitor star with a metallicity similar to that of SN 1986J. To effectively detect and analyze transient X-ray events, a lobster-eye optic array is proposed to significantly enhance the sky coverage of X-ray monitoring. By utilizing an array of optics, with each optic focused on a different position on the detector, a single detector can simultaneously monitor a large portion of the sky for transient sources. This concept can be applied to future facilities with large, wide-field detectors and optical arrays, providing a high degree of spatial resolution and accurate position determination for transient events. This paper presents a design for a proof-of-concept experiment that can be executed using the existing MAXI telescope, with the aim of validating this proposed arrangement and exploring its capabilities. This system can be adapted for other telescopes with similar detectors and optical arrays, and can be a cost-effective way to enhance the capabilities of these instruments. This strategy can also be a precursor for more complex arrangements, with potential applications for future facilities such as the X-ray Telescope Array. This paper is the first in a series and focuses solely on the design and testing of this proposed arrangement, with future papers to concentrate on data analysis and the detection of transient events. A significant portion of very low-mass star-forming cores exhibit complex structures that cannot be explained by their magnetic or gravitational forces alone. While some of these cores may be influenced by external factors such as dynamic interactions with nearby protostars or prestars, most are thought to have local, small-scale variations in density that could be attributed to a self-similar, universal behavior. However, when we examine high-mass star-forming cores, a contrasting pattern emerges where larger, separate dense cores often lie in close proximity to one another before coalescing and contributing to the growth of a single massive protostar. By analyzing the spatial relationships between dense gas cores and assessing their merger rates, we can gain insight into the unique characteristics of massive star formation. Utilizing a 1.1 square degree field of view observed by the Herschel Space Observatory and ATLASGAL, we identified dense gas cores within massive star-forming regions and mapped their spatial distributions to calculate the frequency of core mergers. Based on observed core densities and distances from nearby protostars or formed stars, we estimated the frequency of mergers to be quite high, ranging from 10 to 100 per core, with some even reaching as high as a few hundred. Over the course of a few free-fall times, these projected merger frequencies would result in the formation of massive protostellar clusters similar to those observed in the RCW 106 giant molecular complex. Furthermore, we propose that the extensive core mergers could influence the protostellar mass function by favoring the formation of massive protostars over low-mass ones. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the core accretion model, suggesting that it may be insufficient on its own to explain the formation of very massive stars and that merger-driven growth may be a critical component of massive star formation similar to its role in low-mass star formation. The prevalence of false news is not a new issue but one that is expanding at a rapid pace. By integrating a score function that assesses the credibility of news based on its factual content, our system achieves superior performance in detecting both simple and complex false news. Moreover, we demonstrate that our approach can be applied to existing summarization systems to enhance the accuracy of fake news detection tasks. By deploying this technique on a real-world application, we also showcase a tangible instance of utilizing BART for summarization and evaluating its impact on a fake news detection system. This work investigates the impact of a specific phenomenon called "bending" occurring in stochastic processes, specifically Gaussian random fields, which can be defined as continuous extensions of Gaussian random functions. A particular type of bending is identified where the field's behavior changes significantly as it transitions from a stationary to a locally stationary state. The study demonstrates how this type of bending affects the field's second moments by deriving an analytical formula that accounts for non-stationarity. Furthermore, the research explores the implications of bending for local extreme value statistics by establishing relationships with the maximum of Gaussian processes and extremal process theory. These connections are utilized to develop an algorithm that can simulate stationary fields with prescribed covariance functions, even if exact representation is impossible. The study also compares and contrasts a proposed point-weighted empirical estimator for estimating the field's spectral density at a single point with existing methods, utilizing both simulated data and real data from a geophysical field. The results show that this new estimator performs well and is more efficient than the alternatives. The research presented in this paper is applied to a real-world problem, namely estimating the spectral density of a geophysical field with limited data, which in turn is utilized to simulate a field with the same characteristics as the real one. The findings are then used to create an animated visualization of this simulated field. The paper is concluded by discussing its main contributions, which include developing a new approach for dealing with the bending effect, exploring its implications for local extreme value statistics, and providing an algorithm for simulating stationary fields from their past realizations. The research is also placed within the broader context of the field, which includes related work on extreme value theory, geostatistics, and random field theory. The paper is organized as follows: the introduction sets out the background and motivation for the research presented, while the methods section explains the approach used, which includes a review of the point-weighted empirical estimator and the algorithm for simulating the fields. The results are then discussed, followed by the conclusion. The paper ends with an acknowledgement of the sources of funding and support for the research, as well as a list of references cited. We modify the standard $\ell_1$-PCA problem to achieve rotational invariance by taking the Euclidean norm of the eigenvector, which allows us to apply the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) condition to find the optimal solution. We then employ the iterative reweighting algorithm, similar to $\ell_1$-PCA, to solve the dual problem and obtain an estimate of the optimal eigenvector. We also conduct experiments to compare our method with the state-of-the-art Outlier Pursuit algorithm, demonstrating improved performance in terms of recovery rate. We further analyze a real-world dataset comprising images, showing that our method yields a more accurate representation than the standard $\ell_1$-PCA. We conclude by discussing potential applications and future work on our method. We append an outline of the proof for linear convergence in the appendix. Unknown domains pose a significant challenge for navigation. Amap navigation uses pre-mapped areas for efficient route planning but relies on extensive prior knowledge. Building upon amap navigation, HiTMap introduces a hierarchical topological representation that combines geospatial data with graph-based topology. Each node in the HiTMap represents a specific geographic area, and the edges between them convey critical route planning information obtained through exploration. One of the key limitations in using matter-wave interferometry to detect magnetic fields lies in differentiating interferometry signals resulting from field variations and those produced by interactions with a superconductor through the Meissner effect. In this study, we investigate the use of a specific type of interferometer, where an atomic beam meets a surface and scatters off surface atoms, to overcome this challenge. Due to its high sensitivity to local magnetic fields, this interferometer is capable of distinguishing between the initial condition, where a superconductor is present and the atomic beam scatters off gas molecules instead of the surface, and a situation where the beam interacts directly with the surface but with a superconducting layer blocked by an anti-ferromagnetic layer. By controlling parameters such as atomic beam intensity and width, we find that a detection limit of $10^{-12}$ Tesla can be achieved, which is comparable to the magnitude of fields produced by the Meissner effect and thus enabling the differentiation. This achievement paves the way for using atomic interferometry in precise measurements of local magnetic field variations and the superconducting properties of materials in real-world settings. This detection limit can be further improved by optimizing parameters, allowing for the investigation of superconductor's unique properties such as the upper critical field, pinning field, and the field decay length in the London penetration depth layer. In this work, we examine a mixture model consisting of Gaussian components with varying means and standard deviations for a univariate normal distribution. This model can be reinterpreted using stochastic geometry to depict non-overlapping hyperspheres within a hypersphere whose volume is one, representing all possible data. This representation enables us to apply results from geometric probability to derive estimators for the model's parameters. Additionally, we reframe the model within the framework of Choquet theory to identify its parameter estimator as the expected value of a functional over a specific convex set. This approach allows us to leverage the stability of the model's estimator in relation to its underlying representation. In examining the model's performance through simulations, we find that it compares favorably to other, more complex models used for density estimation. Furthermore, we apply the mixture model to analyze spatial configurations of a point process and determine its parameters using the model's estimators. In doing so, we calculate the expected volume of a sphere containing all points within a given radius as well as the distribution of the radius of the smallest sphere containing all points. Both of these measures provide valuable insights into the point process's properties. We use a mixture model consisting of Gaussian components to estimate these measures, choosing the number of components through cross-validation to ensure accurate representation of the data. We also conduct a simulation study to validate the model's performance in accurately estimating the parameters of a given point process model. We collect and analyze real-world data consisting of the positions of trees in a forest, using the mixture model to estimate the parameters of the point process model from which the data was generated. We find that the model's ability to accurately estimate the parameters of the point process model decreases as the points become more clustered, recommending future research into models that can effectively handle such situations. We believe that the mixture model's ability to capture the characteristics of a point process can be generalized to other types of data, recommending its use as a tool for data analysts. We also recommend further research into the model's performance with increasingly complex data and point processes. Allocating memory efficiently on a GPU is a complex task that can hinder GPU-based object-oriented programming's full potential.  In response to this challenge, researchers have developed various object-oriented programming languages that leverage memory allocation and deallocation to enhance performance and safety.  However, existing GPU memory allocators fail to optimize memory usage and access efficiency for object-based programming.  To address this limitation, we present DynaSOAr, a high-performance parallel memory allocator tailored specifically for object-based programming on modern GPUs.  DynaSOAr's unique blend of first-fit and binary search allocation strategies ensures minimal fragmentation and fast allocation times.  Additionally, the allocator features a compact header format and strategically placed padding to optimize memory access efficiency.  We have implemented DynaSOAr within the CUDA programming model and conducted extensive performance evaluations using both general-purpose and specialized benchmarks.  The results show that DynaSOAr outperforms the default CUDA allocator across a wide range of applications and provides notable improvements in memory usage and access efficiency.  We also present several case studies highlighting DynaSOAr's ability to optimize memory usage and fix common memory-related issues in popular open-source object-oriented applications.  To facilitate seamless integration into existing workflows, we have made DynaSOAr a publicly available open-source tool on GitHub.  With DynaSOAr, developers can now unlock the full potential of GPU-based object-oriented programming, gaining access to significant performance boosts, reduced memory waste, and improved memory safety.  We believe DynaSOAr's innovative design and features will also serve as a valuable reference for the development of future memory allocators and object-oriented programming languages targeting modern GPUs.  We have explored several optimization opportunities and identified performance bottlenecks in various object-oriented applications and demonstrated how DynaSOAr can be effectively integrated into these workloads.  We have further analyzed the implications of DynaSOAr's design choices on memory usage, access efficiency, and fragmentation and presented several case studies highlighting DynaSOAr's ability to fix common memory-related issues in open-source object-oriented applications.  We have also compared DynaSOAr's performance with a state-of-the-art, production-level CUDA-aware CUDA-PMR2 memory allocator and demonstrated how DynaSOAr's unique features can be used to optimize memory usage and fix memory-related issues in various object-oriented applications. The NASA TESS mission's comprehensive all-sector sky coverage allows for a more in-depth examination of exoplanetary systems within the Milky Way. This research involves exploring the 2.5 years' worth of TESS data to identify exoplanet systems consisting of multiple planets around the same star. A new method was developed to detect such systems by focusing on planets with orbital periods of 20 days or less and detecting complete planetary systems by looking for patterns in detected planets. This method uncovered 14 new systems consisting of two planets each. A 3.5-year TESS light curve set was also utilized to develop a new detection technique for exoplanets, leading to the discovery of 149 new planets across 106 stars. This list includes the recently reported TOI-712 system, which features three mini-Neptans and offers promising conditions for potentially hosting life on its innermost planet. A follow-up investigation involving radial velocity measurements from the HARPS instrument confirmed the existence of the three planets and provided more precise mass and orbital period estimates. These findings reinforce the significance of the TESS mission in revealing the intricate details of exoplanetary systems within the Milky Way.

The non-equilibrium dynamics of a massive field in de Sitter space, modelled by a quantum field in interaction with a quantum system, exhibits a fascinating phenomenon where the system's quantum properties lead to an amplification of the quantum fluctuations of the field, even over vast distances. Although this noise enhancement diminishes as the system and field become thermally entangled, it can still significantly grow if the system's temperature is lower than the cosmological temperature. We have investigated this phenomenon in simulations of semi-quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d using qudits, specifically qutrits, which allow us to explore this effect in various scenarios, and have established that the noise increase can be more pronounced when the system and field are in a superposition state rather than being coupled in a single, maximally entangled state. Moreover, we have found that the system's temperature plays a crucial role in this effect, with higher temperatures leading to greater noise enhancement. We have also validated our simulations using a semi-quantum Lindblad approach and semi-classical cosmological quantum field theory, which consistently yield the same outcome. Lastly, we have discussed the practicality of utilizing noise-enhanced qutrits as cosmological probes, which could be executed with current technology in laboratory setups involving up to 10 qutrits.

Research indicates that highly polarized positrons can be generated through interactions between intense laser light and solid materials, specifically in the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. In traditional target media, such as gases and liquids, the degree of polarization achieved is generally limited to a few percent due to the scattered photons being largely unpolarized. However, using a thin solid material, specifically a thin film, as the target could potentially lead to a much higher degree of polarization. A theoretical analysis reveals that a very dense and polarized positron beam can be produced when a solid film is exposed to a high-power laser, with polarization degrees exceeding 90% and the peak positron density reaching $10^{12}$ per cm$^3$ within a solid target over a broad range of laser intensities. This happens as the highest-energy photons are focused on the front surface of the film, resulting in the most intense positron production and maximal polarization. This indicates that using a thin solid film as the target could significantly enhance the efficiency and polarization of positrons produced through laser-plasma interactions. The flow of complex fluids is significantly influenced by surface phenomena due to the high proportion of interface compared to bulk. While the flow of fluids with textured surfaces has been studied extensively, the impact of texture on the surface flow of highly complex liquids, such as liquid foams, is not well understood and is the subject of this study. Using high-speed cameras to observe the flow of liquid foams between two textured plates at varying speeds and distances apart, we have created a theoretical model that accurately explains and predicts observed behavior. By applying the model to a wide range of scenarios, we have identified specific conditions under which increased texture roughness can either increase or decrease friction. Furthermore, we have found that our model aligns with existing theories related to textured surfaces and flow, and has also provided insights into how the configuration of liquid foam lamellae influences friction. By analyzing the configuration of lamellae, we have discovered that the curvature of plate edges can influence the curvature of lamellae curves, leading to a more curved shape in areas further away from the point of plate intersection. This, in turn, contributes to increased friction in these areas. By accounting for this curvature, we have successfully reduced the uncertainty in our model's predictions by a factor of ten. This study highlights the significance of considering the complex internal structure of liquid foams when studying their flow behavior and has implications for the development of models that simulate the flow of similar non-Newtonian liquids. By using a simplified theoretical model, we have also demonstrated that the texture-induced increase in friction in liquid foams can be minimized through the application of a curved surface, thus providing a practical solution that can be implemented in real-world scenarios. Skin cancer diagnosis can be complex due to the irregularity and subjectivity of dermatological images. In addition to this difficulty, treating dermatological images using deep learning techniques can be time-consuming and require significant memory, making them prone to poor performance when new sample types are introduced. In this study, three deep learning-based techniques - Inception, VGG16, and ResNet50 - are applied to dermatological images with different feature extractors to determine the optimal network for diagnosing five skin cancer types. The entropy of the network's final layer features is also utilized to assess the normality of the images and remove those with abnormally low entropy, resulting in a 6.3% improvement in accuracy to 86.3%. When the remaining images are divided into ten subsets, with nine subsets used for training and one subset used for testing, the average accuracy of the models ranges from 73.2% to 84.8%. In order to further evaluate the generalizability of the models, new, unseen dermatological images are captured and processed in real-time using a simplified network, and in both cases, with and without the entropy filter, the models achieve high accuracy of over 80%. In conclusion, using the Inception network with a specific feature extractor yields the best performance and using the entropy of the network's features or capturing images in real-time with limited processing results in similar performance. In practical applications, using the Inception network with the specified feature extractor, capturing images in real-time with minimal processing, or employing a more complex network with sufficient data may produce better outcomes. In addition, the models' ability to distinguish between cancer and healthy skin is straightforward and can be quantified using the entropy of the network's features or the simplicity of the capturing process. In the future, the models can be trained on more dermatological image types and used to detect unusual images as they are captured. The code for this study is available online. The network architecture used in this study can also be adapted for classifying unusual images in other medical fields. The study includes visual explanations of how the models misclassify healthy skin images and provides guidance on capturing dermatological images. In neural machine translation, the focus mechanism allows the source and target languages to influence each other during decoding, leading to improved results by enabling the model to selectively pay attention to specific source words when generating target words. However, this mutual attention can cause circular references, where the model refers to previously generated target words, violating the monotonicity constraint. To mitigate this issue, the focus mechanism is typically set to decay over time. But this simple approach can result in suboptimal translations by constraining the model's ability to revisit important previous words. We propose an innovative look-ahead focus method to address this limitation. Instead of simply decaying the focus, we introduce a forward attention mechanism that allows the model to focus on specific target words at each decoding step, without being restricted by the monotonicity constraint. We further investigate how to initialize the hidden states for this forward attention, exploring different methods to enhance performance. Our proposed approach achieves superior results compared to the baseline method, with significant improvements when translating long sentences. By enabling the model to freely revisit previous target words, we observe a notable increase in the frequency of backward references, from 15.6% to 34.8%. Our code is available online. We believe this research has implications beyond neural machine translation, potentially benefiting other generation tasks subject to similar constraints. To further analyze our proposed approach, we divide the target words that the model refers to using the forward attention into two categories: essential words that are crucial for sentence coherence and whose reuse is permitted under the monotonicity constraint; and redundant words that are not necessary for coherence and whose reuse is forbidden. We observe that the model's focus on these categories is unevenly distributed, with a bias towards essential words when the sentence length increases. To investigate how the model incorporates knowledge about sentence coherence, we design a synthetic task where the model must generate lists of lengths unknown in advance. We find that this ability to handle unknown list lengths is challenging for the model, with performance declining compared to translating single sentences of the same length. We attribute this decline to the difficulty of capturing coherence over lists of unknown lengths, which presents a new research challenge. We propose several potential solutions to this problem, including conditioning the model on the list length, using memory banks to store references to previous elements, or employing external knowledge about typical list lengths. We believe that successful generation in this synthetic task could be an indicator of a model's ability to capture coherence over lists of unknown lengths in real-world translation tasks. The significant progress made in grid computing was not solely the result of technical advancements but was greatly influenced by a theoretical framework known as the Grid Translation Approach. This concept, which combines elements of social constructivism and technology studies, helped define the boundaries and characteristics of grid computing during its development. As a result, the Grid Translation Approach gained a prominent role in guiding development decisions and ultimately contributing to the technology's functionality and appeal to its users. By examining the relationship between technology and its purpose, the Grid Translation Approach provided a valuable lens through which to assess the grid computing paradigm. Consequently, this paper delves into the underlying principles of the Grid Translation Approach and explores its implications for the development of grid computing. Furthermore, it offers insights into this theoretical framework's broader relevance to other computing paradigms, such as cloud computing, distributed systems, and utility computing. By exploring the transformation of grid computing, this paper aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion about the future of these technologies and provide a valuable resource for researchers, developers, and policymakers working within this field. The method's intermediate state, represented by the eigenvectors and eigenvalues from each domain, enables bridge linking with classical spatial analysis through principal component analysis (PCA). A key innovation is the development of a statistical test to evaluate temporal variability across different spatial domains using eigenvalues from each domain, which can be employed to identify linked components even in domains where the data variability is significantly different. The results obtained using the proposed methodological extension are compared with traditional MF-SSA, revealing the benefits of considering spatial information and the importance of domain identification for accurate reconstruction. The methodological extension and statistical tests developed can be applied to other fields involving the analysis of multivariate time series in different spatial domains. We investigate the global behavior of the supremum of the local time of a symmetric one-dimensional random walk whose initial condition is chosen from a specific range. By developing new inequalities and using existing results from the literature, we establish tight bounds on the moment functions of the local time's supremum. These moment functions follow an exponential distribution when the walk's initial condition is zero, but they take on a different form when the walk starts from a non-zero initial condition. This non-zero start case leads to moment functions whose $p$th order is directly proportional to the $p$th power of the absolute value of the walk's initial condition, combined with powers of the square root of the walk's generation time. This proportionality holds regardless of whether the walk's initial condition is positive or negative. This study's random walk model can be viewed as a specific instance of a broader process known as the stochastic Cauchy process, which has been extensively studied in the literature. This process's local time has been analyzed in great detail, but the approach taken here provides an independent proof of the relevant bounds. This convergence was discovered by applying specific moment functions to the walk's height system, and it led to the realization that similar methods could be applied to the local time system. This realization sparked the investigation into the moment functions of the local time system. This research also explored the approach used in the related paper, and it found that the moment functions' convergence could be described using the Ray-Knight theorem. A plasma source called IShTAR has been developed for plasma characterization and study in the context of ITER. It operates in two modes - a helicon and a magnetized plasma, with a separate neutral gas injection system to introduce impurities into the plasma. A combination of optical and electrical measurements were taken to analyze the plasma in both modes, with results showing that the helicon mode produces a plasma with a high electron temperature and neutral gas injection allowing for the study of radiative effects. A code called COLDPF was also utilized to simulate the plasma and a good match was found between simulated and measured data, validating the code's effectiveness. Further improvements to the IShTAR plasma source are also proposed, including a larger plasma chamber and additional magnetic coils, which could make it an advanced test bed for studying edge plasma conditions similar to those found in ITER.

Diagnosis of liver diseases through image analysis relies heavily on accurately identifying nuclei in histopathology images. To automate this process, researchers have explored using deep learning-based methods to detect and segment nuclei from images. However, training such models requires access to large datasets, which can be difficult to obtain due to the sensitive and personal nature of medical data. To circumvent this limitation, we propose a novel convolutional neural network, W-Net, that can detect and segment nuclei from small training sets without the need for explicit classification. In contrast to most existing approaches that use classification-based methods, our network consists of two stages: first, it locates potential nuclei candidates through a binary classification, and then refines these candidates by regressing their masks. The use of a binary classification stage enables the network to focus on distinguishing genuine nuclei from background, thereby improving the quality of the candidates. To evaluate our network, we utilized two publicly available datasets and compared its performance to state-of-the-art approaches, discovering that it surpasses them in accuracy, Dice coefficient, and Inference Time. Moreover, we discovered that training the network on 100 images yields the best results, indicating that it is highly efficient even with limited data. To further enhance its performance, we proposed a novel data augmentation technique called "nucleus copying," which replicates the distribution of nuclei in images by randomly copying them, and demonstrated its effectiveness in boosting the network's performance. Lastly, we applied the network to a manually marked dataset and used the marked nuclei as input to recover the corresponding images, successfully recovering authentic-looking images comprised of diverse shapes and sizes. The simplicity and high efficiency of our network, coupled with its superior performance, make it an ideal solution for real-world applications. The code for the proposed network is available online.

Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have proven highly effective in processing complex graph data and identifying crucial features. However, the inherent complexity of these networks makes it challenging to understand their underlying workings and interpret their output. To address this limitation, we present a novel analysis of GCNNs, revealing that their fundamental operation can be viewed as a matched filtering process in multivariate signal processing. By breaking down the network's operation in this way, we gain a more intuitive understanding of how GCNNs extract valuable information from noisy data and distinguish between important and irrelevant features. This matched filtering perspective provides a practical means of selecting important network components and interpreting the results, as it allows us to evaluate the network's performance using well-established metrics in signal processing. We apply this analysis to a specific GCNN structure, and through numerical experiments, demonstrate its effectiveness in identifying important features and distinguishing between them and irrelevant information. This approach can be readily integrated into existing GCNN frameworks to enhance their performance and interpretability. This research offers a fresh, data-independent perspective on the functioning of GCNNs that complements existing data-driven insights. This approach has the potential to be adapted for other deep learning networks that incorporate learnable filters. We focus on a 3-dimensional Einstein gravity theory that couples a scalar field to Chern-Simons form, a technique that has been effectively utilized in topological gravity theories. We demonstrate that this action is equivalent to a more fundamental action that includes a scalar field and a gauge field in a specific symmetry. We then analyze the properties of these solutions in the context of this more fundamental theory. We find that the solutions can be described as solitons rather than black holes, as they do not meet the criteria for black holes. Elastography, an imaging technique that utilizes tissue stiffness information to diagnose diseases, is highly susceptible to axial motion artifacts. While the synthetic aperture approach has effectively mitigated axial motion effects by focusing on data sampled in the aperture time frame, its limitations in the lateral direction have hindered a similar advancement. The Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture technique presented here overcomes these constraints by employing the virtual source synthetic aperture method in both the axial and lateral directions to accurately determine tissue displacement and differentiation in elastography, even in the presence of significant lateral shifts. By utilizing the precise information available from the sample aperture time frame, this approach achieves superior performance compared to conventional synthetic aperture techniques, as demonstrated by simulation, phantom, and in vivo studies. The resulting algorithm is computationally efficient and straightforward to implement, making it a valuable addition to the elastography community. The technique has been applied to actual elastography data and yields notable improvements in image quality, as quantified by both qualitative and quantitative assessments. The elastography contrast-to-noise ratio is observed to increase by 2.5 dB, while the mean absolute error in stiffness estimation is found to decrease by 1.5 dB when employing the Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture technique. The technique's broad applicability is further highlighted by its suitability for a wide range of ultrasound systems. The Virtual Source Synthetic Aperture approach offers a promising solution for addressing lateral motion issues in elastography, as well as in other medical imaging modalities that rely on the synthetic aperture technique. The algorithm's versatility makes it a valuable tool for a broad range of applications, including but not limited to cardiac elastography, abdominal imaging, and musculoskeletal imaging, in addition to various non-medical imaging scenarios. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. Our new "Vector Boson Approximation" (VBA) approach simplifies the calculation by treating the scattering of a lepton and a vector boson as equivalent to the scattering of two fermions with the same total momentum. In solving inverse problems, researchers and engineers aim to restore a degraded or incomplete signal. This process involves estimating the underlying data, given a partially observed and disturbed version of it. We developed a regularized conditional GAN, or $\textfrak{c}$-GAN, to tackle such issues by combining the benefits of both regularized and conditional GANs. These models typically enhance the quality of restored images and provide a meaningful latent space, respectively. We leveraged the $\textfrak{c}$-GAN's unique characteristics to solve posterior estimation problems by training the model using prior samples and observed data. This resulted in a data-driven prior distribution that accurately captures the solution's characteristics and minimizes overestimation, thereby yielding restored solutions closest to the true solutions. We demonstrated and validated the effectiveness of this approach through extensive numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world data. These experiments showed that the $\textfrak{c}$-GAN yields superior reconstruction quality compared to standard techniques used in signal processing. Moreover, by applying the $\textfrak{c}$-GAN to real-world image deconvolution problems, we achieved state-of-the-art results comparable to cutting-edge machine learning techniques used for image reconstruction. The developed $\textfrak{c}$-GAN framework provides a versatile tool for solving a wide range of inverse problems involving non-Gaussian noise. This difficult problem, which we've termed VBL (unknown linear transformation-based noise localization), has previously been approached using methods like sparse representation or low-rank representation, but not optimal estimation techniques like Maximum Likelihood Estimation, MAP, or ML2. In this paper, we propose a novel VBL algorithm based on the ML2 criterion, which we call ML2-Blind, designed to locate the noises in an overcomplete dictionary with linear transformations, with the goal of minimizing the number of errors in the noise locations. Moreover, we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of the ML2-Blind algorithm to real-world problems, including blind source separation and image deblurring. Recently, graph neural networks have achieved significant performance in various tasks such as node classification and link prediction. However, most current methods rely on Euclidean distances between nodes, which may not accurately capture their complex relationships in many real-world applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel GNN architecture that utilizes Lorentzian distances to characterize the relationships between nodes. By leveraging the non-symmetric and space-time based properties of Lorentzian distances, our method can effectively capture the directional and temporal aspects of graphs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by applying it to task such as predicting the orientation of satellites and analyzing the temporal patterns in citation networks. Compared to existing methods and a randomly selected baseline, our model achieves superior results in these applications. We also evaluate our approach on publicly available datasets and find it outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by a notable margin. Our code is available online.

To address this issue, we first need to solve a direct problem that involves solving a wave equation in the air and a partial differential equation in the solid, taking into account the interface where the two media meet. Once this direct problem is solved, we can determine the surface measurements of the sound wave in the air. To solve the inverse problem, we use a method known as the Tikhonov regularization to minimize the difference between the calculated sound wave and the measured sound wave in the air, while also accounting for any prior knowledge about the location and severity of the cracks. To validate this method, we use numerical simulations to simulate a situation where a crack appears in an object and measure the sound waves in the air above it, and then use this data to try to locate and determine the severity of the crack. This process is repeated for different sizes and shapes of cracks and in the presence of random noise in the sound wave measurements. variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to a Tsallis $q$-exponential model.
We derive the impulsivity parameter's expression and examine how it relates
to traditional delay discounting models by conducting a series of numerical
experiments using both real and artificially generated data sets. Our results show
that the proposed model accurately captures the relationship between the $q$-exponential
and exponential delay discounting impulsivity parameters. Furthermore, we
determine the optimal $q$ value that minimizes the mean squared error between
the $q$-exponential and the proposed model, finding it to be approximately 3.3
for the majority of scenarios. We also explore the connection between the proposed
model and utility functions, discovering that its $q$-exponential form can be
reinterpreted as a logarithmic utility function when the delay period equals
one. Our analysis suggests that the proposed model provides a suitable alternative
to the commonly employed exponential delay discounting model. Ultimately, our
model offers a valuable tool for examining the relationship between impulsivity
and delay discounting, with implications for psychological and neuroscience research.

Using AI-based image editing for assistance is beneficial, especially when combined with safe and simple procedures. In the context of healthcare, particularly with chest X-rays, editing images that contain medical information requires extreme caution to avoid misleading diagnoses. Previously, research focused on generating synthetic X-rays to train AI models, prioritizing diversity over similarity to actual images. However, this approach can lead to the creation of overfitting models that are prone to producing diagnoses that are too optimistic, and as a result, do not adequately account for data uncertainty. To address this challenge, researchers developed a method to train robust models that prioritize data diversity and capture uncertainty, which in turn enables secure image editing capabilities. By leveraging the diversity of the generated data and Adversarial Training, a method was developed to train models that can safely edit chest X-rays without compromising the integrity of the images. To evaluate the model's performance, researchers conducted experiments on actual image editing tasks using both naive and sophisticated editing techniques. The results showed that the models' performance can be accurately evaluated using metrics that assess the similarity between the edited and original images, which in turn supports reliable decision-making about the safety of the models. To take it a step further, researchers developed an approach to assess the models' ability to capture uncertainty, which in turn enables the development of more precise editing techniques that prioritize the preservation of the images' integrity. To demonstrate the practical applications of the models, researchers conducted editing tasks that simulated the removal of medical conditions, which in turn supported the evaluation of the models using both subjective and objective assessment criteria. The results of the experiments have significant implications for the development of secure and reliable methods for editing chest X-rays, which in turn can be used to support decision-making in healthcare settings. The research also highlights the importance of accounting for data uncertainty and diversity when training models that can safely edit medical images. To achieve this, researchers proposed a method that combines the use of adversarial loss functions and noise injection to capture the uncertainty of the data and diversity of the generated samples, which in turn enables the development of secure and reliable methods for editing chest X-rays. To further validate the models, researchers conducted additional experiments on a second dataset that consisted of lung nodules, which in turn supported the evaluation of the models using both qualitative and quantitative assessment criteria. Researchers often work with high-dimensional data in various fields including physics. A new tool, ViDaExpert, is developed to visualize and analyze multidimensional vectorial data by applying three main methods: direct visualization of vectors, projection based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), and flow visualization. The tool allows users to easily perform and adjust calculations, facilitating an intuitive comprehension of complex high-dimensional data. ViDaExpert, designed to operate within the Python environment, builds upon the base functionality of ViDa by incorporating an interactive graphical user interface using the Qt framework and the matplotlib library for visualization purposes. The tool's capabilities are demonstrated through applications in physics, specifically in the analysis of high-speed camera measurements and simplified fluid dynamics simulations. By leveraging ViDaExpert's features, researchers can efficiently explore and gain insights from large-scale simulations, further facilitated by the ability to import data from popular simulation software including OpenFOAM and PALM. The tool along with user guidelines is made available online to promote data analysis and visualization within the scientific community.
